template_description: Each task is a one-liner 'terminal automation' request phrased as a natural-language shell task (find/grep/tar-style filtering, MAC extraction, dedup counting, etc.) on top of small seeded fixture files, with the agent required to capture combined stdout/stderr of a single shell session to /output/command_capture.txt. The verifier (tests/verifier.py) loads a golden expected_output string from tests/verifier_data.json, normalizes both actual and expected text (strips ANSI codes, path prefixes, size units, whitespace) into a line multiset, and passes only if every expected 'record' is present and no unexpected line contains an error keyword. The agent only ever sees instruction.md and setup_files/ (seed fixtures plus setup_seeds.sh); tests/ (including the golden verifier_data.json and solution/solve.sh) is not copied into the Dockerfile image, so the oracle answer is not visible to the agent at solve time. The Dockerfile installs a generic Ubuntu 24.04 + build-essential + python3 + git/curl/wget toolchain; almost none of it is essential since every observed solution is a single bash pipeline of coreutils (grep/find/sort/uniq/tr/diff/readlink/printf/cat).
unlock_notes: Nearly all tasks are already shellsim_now=yes; a couple lean on grep -f (pattern file) or the coreutils `diff` utility, which shellsim's Real coreutils list does not currently include — filling those gaps in the existing grep/find partial implementations would cover the remainder rather than requiring a whole new capability tier.
quality_notes: Individually trivial and highly template-generated (single canned bash one-liner per task), but well-specified and easy to verify exactly since the golden output is hidden from the agent and the fuzzy line-multiset comparison is reasonably strict about missing records and error keywords. One task (task_7196) is oddly self-defeating: the instruction tells the agent to fabricate the 'network interface info' file itself before printing it, so success reduces to reproducing literal text the agent invents, not to real system inspection. No leaked solutions or golden answers were found in the agent-visible file set.

template_description: Each task is a competitive-programming problem (AtCoder/Codeforces/AOJ style, drawn from DeepMind's CodeContests) presented as a full problem statement, and the agent must write a self-contained, non-blocking Python solution to /app/solution.py that reads all of stdin at once and prints to stdout. The verifier (tests/test_state.py, run via pytest) shells out to `python3 /app/solution.py` for each of 5-10 stored input strings (tests/test_data.json) with a 30s per-case timeout, and asserts the stripped, line-split stdout matches the stored expected output exactly; test.sh always writes reward.txt (0 or 1) even on pytest failure. No solution/ directory or oracle code is present anywhere in the agent-visible task tree, and tests/ is not copied into the Dockerfile image (only installed at verification), so the golden answers are not leaked. The Dockerfile installs Ubuntu 24.04 with python3/pip and pre-installs pytest/pytest-json-ctrf purely for the verifier's own use; nothing beyond a bare python3 interpreter is needed by the agent's solution.
unlock_notes: Agent side needs a real Python interpreter with standard-library modules (sys, math, itertools, collections, bisect, etc. depending on the problem) capable of running on unbounded-size actual solution code, not the current print/assign/arithmetic shim; the verifier itself is a host-side subprocess+string-compare harness that is otherwise portable once such an interpreter exists.
quality_notes: Difficulty and interest vary a lot by problem (from a one-line permutation check to real DP/greedy/binary-search algorithms), and problems with only 5 test cases overlapping the visible sample in instruction.md are the most susceptible to shallow special-casing/hardcoding rather than genuine algorithm implementation; problems with 10 more varied cases (e.g. modular-inverse, binary-search+greedy tasks) are meaningfully harder to hack. No leaked solutions or defects were found; the test.sh's set+e/set-e reward handling correctly avoids the RewardFileNotFoundError failure mode it documents fixing.

template_description: A 'code_gen_with_tests' family (mix of real algorithm problems, small helper utilities, and fake mock-library implementations of real third-party APIs like rpy2, ansys.dpf, or metaspace) each verified by a dedicated tests/test_adversarial.py run under pytest with strict timeouts, JUnit reporting, and a reward.txt written from a case analysis of the pytest exit code (0=pass, 1/2=scored zero, other=hard failure). tests/ (including test_adversarial.py) is not copied into the Dockerfile image, so hidden tests are not directly visible to the agent, though several instructions describe test behavior in enough narrative detail to functionally leak the test intent. The Dockerfile installs Ubuntu 24.04 with python3/pip plus a fixed bundle of pytest, pytest-asyncio, pytest-mock, requests-mock, pytest-aiohttp/aiohttp, and pytest-console-scripts — most tasks use only a small slice of this (plain pytest, or one of packaging/numpy which are not explicitly installed and may rely on being already present in the base image or as transitive deps).
unlock_notes: Baseline need is a real Python interpreter that can execute arbitrary user modules under pytest (threading, functools, argparse, subprocess, regex all stdlib); several tasks additionally require pure-Python third-party packages (pytest itself, packaging, requests-mock/aiohttp for the HDA broker task) and a few (Tic-Tac-Toe AI, metaspace mock, MindSpore mock analog in the other source) require actual NumPy, which is python_native_pkgs and likely out of reach.
quality_notes: Quality is highly bimodal: several tasks (VisibleString ASN.1 encoder, LeetCode Jump Game VII, multiples-of-3-or-5) are well-defined, genuinely verifiable coding exercises with reasonable hack resistance. Others are fake-library mocking tasks (rpy2, ansys.dpf, metaspace) where the 'correct' behavior is arbitrary and reverse-engineerable straight from the visible test assertions, so they mostly test whether the agent can read tests carefully rather than solve a real problem. One task (5k-adversarial-0999) is a severe defect: its instruction openly hands the agent the exact reward-hacking strategy (write a conftest.py that force-empties submit.txt) needed to pass an otherwise-unseen test, and even the referenced test name ('test_success') doesn't match the actual hidden test file's function names — a template/generation mismatch on top of an already degenerate task.

template_description: A 'curriculum-easy' family of deliberately simplified Python coding tasks, each asking the agent to build one small, self-contained module or package under /app (helpers, string-processing heuristics, tiny data classes, or minimal mock stand-ins for real third-party libraries like MindSpore, DaCe, or virtualenv) verified by a dedicated tests/test_curriculum.py run under pytest, with a trap-based test.sh that always writes reward.txt (1 on success, 0 otherwise). Tests are not copied into the Dockerfile image, so exact hidden assertions are not visible to the agent, though the instructions typically spell out the required API and, often, the literal example inputs/outputs the tests check. The Dockerfile is minimal and consistent across the family: python:3.10-slim plus `pip install pytest`; nothing else is installed, so any task actually needing NumPy or other third-party packages (several do) is relying on packages not present in this image.
unlock_notes: Most tasks need only a real Python interpreter with stdlib (functools, subprocess, argparse, dict/class basics) — no third-party packages — so python_interp alone unlocks the majority. A minority (NumPy-based polytope math, a MindSpore-mock task) need python_native_pkgs and cannot run without it; one task (virtualenv stand-in) may need subprocess/long_process semantics if its hidden tests actually spawn real venvs.
quality_notes: Consistently low-to-moderate interest by design ('easy' curriculum) with mostly crisp, narrow specs; several tasks give away the exact expected outputs for the handful of cases the tests check (e.g. the ingredient-stemming task lists all four literal test strings and their answers), so passing is closer to satisfying a lookup table than implementing a general algorithm — moderate hack risk from over-specification rather than from a broken verifier. One concrete defect: the hash-table task instructs the agent to write /app/hash_table.py, but its test imports 'from app.hash_table import ...', which actually requires a nested app/ package the instruction never mentions — an import-path mismatch that would fail even a fully correct implementation placed where the instructions say.

template_description: Each task asks the agent to reimplement, from scratch and using only the Python standard library, a tiny stand-in for a real third-party library's public API (a beam solver, a WSGI framework, typedpy, fastai, py.path, an ML packaging façade, etc.), as a single file or small package under /app, so that a pytest suite passes. The verifier (tests/test.sh) runs pytest against tests/test_curriculum.py and writes reward.txt from the exit code. Critically, an identical copy of that exact test file is placed at /setup_files/test_curriculum.py, and the instruction explicitly tells the agent to copy or run it from there while developing, so the full literal test assertions (including any hardcoded numeric/string fixtures) are visible to the agent at solve time. The agent only needs a real Python interpreter (classes, sometimes metaclasses, sys.modules injection to fake submodules) and no third-party packages beyond stdlib; the verifier needs pytest. The Dockerfile installs a large scientific/web stack (numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, pillow, requests, matplotlib, etc.) that is essentially unused padding since every instruction insists on stdlib-only solutions.
unlock_notes: Needs a real embedded Python interpreter with class/metaclass support, sys.modules manipulation for fake submodules, decimal, and general stdlib file/text handling, plus pytest to actually execute the leaked test file as the verifier.
quality_notes: Individually well-specified (the instructions are long and precise, and match the leaked test file exactly), but because the exact pytest file is duplicated into the agent-visible /setup_files directory, a policy can special-case the leaked literal fixtures instead of writing a general implementation. Genuine engineering interest is low-to-moderate for most tasks (glue code that mirrors a spec line-by-line); a couple (the WSGI micro-framework, py.path.local subset) require somewhat broader API surfaces and are more interesting. No outright instruction/verifier contradictions were found in this sample.

template_description: Each task is a tiny, self-contained single-function-or-class Python coding exercise (a Calculator class, sum-of-evens, rectangle area, average, bank account, arithmetic dispatcher, etc.) to be written to /app/solution.py. The verifier (tests/test.sh) runs pytest against tests/test_solution.py and writes reward.txt from the exit code; there is no leaked test copy anywhere in the agent-visible tree and no solution/ directory, so the agent only has instruction.md to work from. The agent needs nothing beyond writing a plain Python file (no third-party imports required by any sampled task); the Dockerfile installs pytest, pytest-timeout, beautifulsoup4, requests and flask, none of which are exercised by these tasks — pure unused padding. Instructions are short, concrete, and include worked example cases, generally matching the hidden tests closely.
unlock_notes: Needs a real embedded Python interpreter capable of running normal class/function definitions and pytest to execute the hidden per-task test file; no third-party packages required by the sample.
quality_notes: Very low task interest (boilerplate CRUD-level coding exercises) but generally crisp and well-defined, with no test leakage and a broad enough input space that hardcoding answers is impractical. One clear defect found: two sibling tasks (e2egit-4748, and e2egit-v2's e2egit-0495) have a test_divide with a bare `assert calc.divide(x, 0)` left outside the pytest.raises block, so a correct divide-by-zero implementation makes that line itself raise and the test can never pass — likely a template generation bug that recurs across the family.

template_description: Nearly identical to the sibling e2egit-large family: small self-contained Python coding exercises (mostly a Calculator class, plus a to-do list and an auth system) with no leaked test copy and no solution files, verified by pytest against tests/test_solution.py via the standard test.sh reward.txt wrapper. The key difference from e2egit-large is that instructions in this source frequently say only 'implement in the /app/ directory' without naming the required file, while the hidden test's import statement (sometimes with a giveaway comment like '# Assuming the class is in calculator.py') is the only place the exact required filename appears — an underspecification not present in e2egit-large's solution.py convention. The Dockerfile is identical to e2egit-large's (pytest, pytest-timeout, bs4, requests, flask), all unused padding for these tasks.
unlock_notes: Needs a real embedded Python interpreter and pytest to run the hidden test file; no third-party packages required by any sampled task.
quality_notes: Same low interest, boilerplate level as e2egit-large. Notable defects in this sample: (1) e2egit-0244 is a severe instruction/verifier mismatch — the instruction describes a full Flask REST API with JWT auth endpoints, but the hidden test imports plain functions register_user/login_user/logout_user from app.auth with dict-based responses and custom exceptions, so following the instruction literally cannot pass; (2) e2egit-0495 repeats the e2egit-large family's bare-assert-before-pytest.raises bug in test_divide, making it unpassable even with a correct implementation; (3) several Calculator tasks (0470, 0155, 0183, 0298, 0456) never state the required filename (calculator.py) in the instruction, leaving it to be inferred from a comment buried in the hidden test; (4) e2egit-0464's hidden test requires silently excluding bool values from a numeric sum, an edge case the instruction never mentions; (5) e2egit-0401's logout test only checks that the user remains in user_db, so it does not actually verify session-clearing behavior.

template_description: Each task merges three originally-unrelated small coding tasks (e.g. a random-number/download utility, a CSV/permissions/config processor, and a file-relocation or deletion orchestrator) into one cohesive three-module Python project under /app (core.py, processor.py, integration.py) with an explicit core->processor->integration dependency chain, all stdlib-only, 30-80 lines per module. The verifier runs pytest against tests/test_multifile.py via the standard test.sh reward.txt wrapper. As in the curriculum-medium family, an identical copy of the exact test file is placed at /setup_files/test_multifile.py and the instruction explicitly directs the agent to develop against it, so the literal test assertions (including any monkeypatched network/RNG behavior) are visible at solve time. The agent needs a real Python interpreter (os.walk, subprocess, csv, sometimes urllib.request) but no third-party packages; the Dockerfile installs the same large, mostly-unused scientific/data stack (numpy, pandas, scipy, sklearn, pillow, requests, matplotlib, etc.) seen in curriculum-medium-v2.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Python interpreter with os.walk/subprocess/csv/urllib.request support (network calls are monkeypatched in the leaked tests, so no real net_service is required) plus pytest to run the leaked test file as the verifier.
quality_notes: More substantial than the single-module curriculum-medium tasks — three interdependent modules with real cross-module data flow give genuinely higher interesting scores (3-4) — but the same test-leakage pattern (identical copy in /setup_files) means a policy can hardcode outputs for the leaked tmp_path fixtures instead of writing general recursive file/CSV/RNG logic. Tasks built around randomness or Monte Carlo simulation (e2egit-3311, multifile-3298) are the highest hack risk since seeded/mocked RNG values in the leaked test can be memorized directly. No instruction/verifier contradictions found in this sample.

template_description: Each task asks the agent to implement a small C++ class/module family (image sprites, message queues, config generators, CLI tools, etc.) under /app so that a GoogleTest suite in /tests passes. The Dockerfile is gcc:13 plus cmake/libgtest-dev, built at image time. Critically, every test_solution.cpp we inspected already defines its own full reference implementation of the required classes/functions inline (not extern declarations), and test.sh only links in .cpp files it finds directly under /app (maxdepth 1, no CMakeLists.txt provided) before compiling test_solution.cpp with gtest. The agent's code is therefore never invoked by the test binary; an empty /app already produces a passing build. Tests and (in the one case with a solution/ folder) any reference material are baked into the image and visible to the agent.
unlock_notes: Even with a native C++ compiler in shellsim, this template's tests are self-verifying and ignore the agent's code, so unlocking compiled_lang would not make the tasks meaningful -- the verifier itself needs to be rewritten (e.g. to link the test file against extern-declared agent symbols) before this source is worth using for RL.
quality_notes: Systemic defect across the whole source: hack_risk is maximal because doing nothing at all passes every task. Task descriptions themselves are reasonably concrete and varied (SDL sprites, SQS queues, mbed config, AWS CLI injection, ventilation sim, Open3D models), so the prose looks plausible, but the verifier wiring is broken. Not usable as-is without fixing test.sh to actually exercise agent code.

template_description: Single-function Python competitive-programming tasks: the agent writes one function into /app/solution.py, and a pytest unittest.TestCase in /tests/test_solution.py imports it and checks a handful of concrete input/output cases. The Dockerfile is python:3.10-slim with pytest pre-installed; test.sh falls back to copying the first .py file in /app to solution.py if the agent used a different filename. A solution/solution.py reference file exists in every task directory but is not copied into the agent's image (only present in the harvested task bundle for scoring/comparison). Some instructions (e.g. the circle-area-ratio and prime-frequency tasks) embed the complete reference implementation verbatim in the prose, turning those specific tasks into transcription rather than reasoning exercises; others (graph/DP/combinatorics problems) only give the spec plus a worked numeric example, requiring real algorithm design.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Python interpreter with basic stdlib (math, itertools, collections) to execute agent-written solutions and pytest to run the assertions; no third-party packages beyond pytest are required, and pytest itself could be replaced by a simpler assertion harness if pytest isn't ported.
quality_notes: Well-defined and low hack risk except where the full solution is leaked in the instructions (roughly 2 of the 11 tasks sampled), which flattens those specific tasks to near-trivial copying. The harder combinatorics/graph tasks (MST median, safe nodes, prime-frequency subsequence counting) are genuinely interesting and crisply verified against concrete cases, though some (parking-lot ways, dish ranking, triangle tie-breaking) under-specify edge cases relative to what the hidden tests likely check.

template_description: Same template as pymethods2test-large-v2: a single Python function is implemented in /app/solution.py and checked by a pytest suite in /tests/test_solution.py against concrete cases, on a python:3.10-slim image with pytest pre-installed. A solution/solution.py reference exists per task but is not baked into the agent's build image. In the sampled batch, none of the instructions leaked the full solution verbatim (unlike some large-v2 tasks); each gives only the spec, constraints, and usually one worked example, so genuine algorithm implementation is required.
unlock_notes: Same requirement as the sibling pymethods2test-large-v2 source: a Python interpreter with basic stdlib and a pytest-equivalent assertion runner.
quality_notes: Cleaner than the large-v2 sibling in this batch -- no leaked solutions observed, well-defined specs with examples, low hack risk since the function names/behaviors are concrete and unittest assertions are exact. Interestingness varies from trivial string formatting (like-message generator) to real DP/combinatorics (abc-subsequence counting with wildcards).

template_description: Tasks ask the agent to reimplement a small slice of a real open-source Python package's API (e.g. Fury graphics shaders, ROS2 launch descriptions, uproot, ctd, returns, pcwawc, a Turbine model) as a standalone module/package under /app, driven by a genuine (often lightly adapted) pytest test file copied from that project. The environment is ubuntu:24.04 with python3/pip/venv installed via apt at container start (test.sh creates a venv and installs pytest at verification time); no solution/ directory is present in any sampled task, so no reference implementation leaks into the agent's environment. Verification runs pytest against /tests/test_solution.py with PYTHONPATH=/app.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Python interpreter with a broader stdlib slice than the pymethods2test sources (dataclasses, abc, json, typing, sometimes numpy for the Fury task) plus a pytest-equivalent runner; the Fury task specifically needs numpy, which would require python_pure_pkgs/python_native_pkgs rather than a bare interpreter.
quality_notes: This is the most interesting and best-specified of the three sources sampled: instructions closely mirror real upstream test suites (e.g. the ROS2 launch test file has actual copyright headers) so behavior is unambiguous and hack risk is low -- reward requires a genuinely working reimplementation, not keyword matching. One task (uproot HTTP open()) is ambiguous about whether verification hits a real network target or a mock, which is a fidelity risk worth flagging for portability.

template_description: Each task asks the agent to implement a single self-contained Python function (algorithmic/competitive-programming style, drawn from what looks like a UnitSyn-mined corpus of real solved problems) and write it to /app/solution.py. Verification is a fixed pytest unittest file under /tests/test_solution.py that imports 'from solution import *' and asserts exact outputs against hand-picked example cases; test.sh installs pytest, falls back to copying any stray .py file in /app to solution.py if the agent used a different filename, runs pytest, and writes reward.txt from the exit code. The agent needs nothing beyond a real Python interpreter with stdlib; the verifier is likewise pure Python and needs to execute the agent's code directly. An oracle solution/solution.py is present in the task bundle but is not copied into the Docker image or otherwise exposed to the agent at runtime, so it does not leak. The Dockerfile just installs python:3.10-slim plus pytest, which is essential since the verifier runs real pytest against the agent's file.
unlock_notes: needs a real Python interpreter capable of running arbitrary user-defined functions/classes plus the unittest/pytest machinery (or a harness that swaps in shellsim's own equality checks); no third-party libraries beyond pytest are required by any sampled task.
quality_notes: Difficulty and spec clarity vary noticeably within the source: many tasks (interest calc, string validation, binary addition) are crisp toy exercises with tight specs (well_defined 4-5, interesting 1-2), while a few (modular ModFraction/expected-weight recursion, custom hash function, chef-of-the-year vote tally) are either genuinely harder or have truncated/underspecified prose that leaves real ambiguity resolved only by the hidden tests. Hack risk is low across the board since the verifier actually executes the agent's function against concrete example-based assertions and the oracle solution isn't visible; the main soft risk is that some instructions describe formulas vaguely enough that only the sample assertions pin down real behavior.

template_description: Same family and template as exp_rpt_unitsyn-python-large-v2: single-function Python algorithmic tasks written to /app/solution.py, verified by a fixed unittest-style pytest file that imports the solution and checks concrete example outputs. The test.sh script is nearly identical (installs pytest, falls back to the first .py file if solution.py is missing, runs pytest, writes reward.txt) but omits the explicit PYTHONPATH export used in the large-v2 variant, relying instead on 'cd /app' plus a leading 'sys.path.insert' in the test file. The agent needs only a Python interpreter and stdlib; the verifier needs the same to execute the agent's code and run pytest. No solution/oracle files were observed being copied into the image. The Dockerfile (python:3.10-slim + pytest) is minimal and essential for the verifier.
unlock_notes: same as the sibling source: a real Python interpreter running user functions plus pytest/unittest assertion machinery; no third-party packages beyond pytest needed.
quality_notes: This batch skews toward harder, more classic competitive-programming problems (Dijkstra shortest paths, counting 'abc' subsequences with wildcards mod 1e9+7, range queries on 'good sets') alongside a couple of trivial one-liners (a boolean gate function). Several instructions in this sample are visibly truncated mid-sentence (the sandglass query semantics, the nested expression grouping rule, the 'good set' predicate, and the road-condition parameters in the graph task), which lowers well_defined scores since real behavior is only pinned down by the hidden test file the agent cannot see. Hack risk stays low throughout because tests execute the real function against concrete expected values.

template_description: Each task presents a real open-source project file with a documented static-analysis (Infer) bug finding — bug class, qualifier text, buggy method, and full before-fix source — mostly Java with some C#, drawn from the InferredBugs dataset. The agent must write the 'complete, corrected version' of the named file to a specific path under /app. The verifier (test_state.py, pure Python stdlib) locates the target file, brace-counts to extract the body of one named method, and regex-searches that body for a specific narrow fix signature (e.g. 'public synchronized void reset(', or a null-check on a particular variable) rather than compiling or running any code. test.sh does nothing but apt-get update/install python3-pip and invoke the verifier directly. No solution files are shipped in the bundle. The Dockerfile installs only python3/python3-pip on ubuntu:24.04 — no Java, Maven, .NET, or any compiler for the language actually being 'fixed', so this install is essential for the verifier's Python harness but the task's stated language is never actually built or executed.
unlock_notes: the agent side needs nothing beyond writing a text file to a path (text_only/shell_only suffices, e.g. 'mkdir -p ... && cat > file <<EOF'); the verifier itself is pure Python stdlib text/regex processing over the written file and could run against shellsim's VFS today.
quality_notes: Extremely hackable across the entire sample: because nothing is ever compiled or executed, the pass condition reduces to a single regex or small set of regexes matching inside one extracted method body. An agent can reuse the original buggy method almost verbatim and insert just the keyword/pattern the verifier looks for (e.g. add 'synchronized' to a method signature, or add a syntactically-present but semantically dead null check) without producing correct or even compilable code. This also means the underlying real-world bug fixes (thread-safety, null-dereference) are interesting and well-documented in the instructions, but well_defined and hack_risk are both compromised by a verifier far shallower than the task's apparent ambition. No defects beyond this systemic issue were found — file paths and target methods are always concretely specified and consistent with the buggy source shown.

template_description: A heterogeneous grab-bag of Python coding tasks rather than a single template: some are small original-style unit-test exercises (Calculator, Inventory, Mars days-off formula), some are reimplementation-from-spec tasks that ask the agent to recreate a slice of a real third-party open-source package (socotra_marketplace_helpers, autolamella, pdoc, paramak) well enough to pass that package's actual upstream pytest suite, and one is a mislabeled CrossCodeEval-style 'finish this snippet' prompt whose shipped verifier doesn't check the snippet at all. test.sh across the family installs pytest (+pytest-timeout for some) plus a fixed whitelist of common third-party packages via best-effort pip installs, then runs pytest against /tests/test_solution.py and writes reward.txt from the exit code; none of these tasks ship an oracle solution in the bundle. Dockerfiles vary from a bare python:3.10-slim to ubuntu:24.04 with a venv plus a larger package whitelist (numpy/pandas/django/etc.), and the installs are necessary only insofar as a given task's real test suite imports those libraries.
unlock_notes: most tasks need only python_interp; a few (auth/JWT class, package-reimplementation tasks referencing real libraries) would want python_pure_pkgs (e.g. a jwt-signing shim, warnings/importlib machinery) to be faithfully reproducible, though tests in this sample mostly stayed within stdlib-reachable behavior.
quality_notes: Quality is uneven and this source has the sharpest defects in the batch: one task (0127) has an instruction about a nontrivial Django/pandas code completion but a verifier that only checks the solution module imports and defines something, making it trivially hackable; another (0299) ships a test file whose critical dependency (autoscript_sdb_microscope_client) is never installed, so pytest.importorskip silently skips every real assertion and the task passes with two near-stub functions despite an elaborate spec; a third (0872) copies a real upstream test suite that calls interactive input() and expects live-looking network/JWT config, which can fail for reasons unrelated to the agent's code. The straightforward original-style exercises (Calculator, Inventory, Mars formula) are clean and well-specified with low hack risk. Overall this source needs the most scrutiny of the four before use as an RL target.

template_description: Self-instruct-generated single-file shell/scripting benchmarks on an Ubuntu 24.04 image with common CLI tools installed. Each task asks the agent to write one shell (or trivial Python) script/log satisfying a narrow, concretely specified operation (patch files, delete by glob/depth, print a random string, run a mini Kalman filter). The verifier is a Python test_state.py that locates the agent's deliverable by a small set of candidate paths, then re-executes it against a freshly constructed fixture (or, in one observed case, ignores the agent entirely and re-runs its own reference commands) and writes reward.txt. Dockerfile installs a broad, mostly unnecessary general-purpose toolchain (build-essential, git, poppler-utils, etc.) beyond what any single task needs.
unlock_notes: Nearly all tasks are pure bash/coreutils (find, sed, rm, mktemp, nl, base64) already in shellsim's supported set; the one network-fetch task (curl to example.com) needs net_service with the exact page pre-registered.
quality_notes: Highly variable quality: most tasks are simple, well-specified, script-replay-verified shell exercises with low hack risk (verifier reconstructs fresh fixtures and reruns the agent's own script). At least one task (venv creation/teardown) has a serious defect where the verifier never inspects any agent artifact and simply re-runs its own commands, making the reward independent of agent behavior. The random-string task is also weakly verified (checks for a substring reference plus output format, not true randomness).

template_description: Real GitHub issue/PR pairs across many languages (Julia, Go, JS/TS, Python) turned into SWE-bench-style tasks: the agent must clone the pinned commit of a real OSS repo inside the container, reproduce/understand the reported bug, and edit the source to fix it. The verifier's test.sh applies a hidden test_patch.diff (the tests introduced by the actual fix PR, not visible to the agent beforehand) and runs the project's real test suite via language-specific tooling (Pkg.test, go test, npm test, pytest), grading FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS test name lists via a shared test_state.py/pytest-ctrf harness. A solution/solve.sh oracle patch exists per task but lives outside the agent's build context and /tests is only mounted at verification time, so neither the fix nor the hidden tests are visible to the agent. Dockerfiles install the language runtime for the given project plus a generic apt layer (git, curl, build-essential) needed to clone and build real repositories.
unlock_notes: Needs live git clone of large real-world repositories, a real compiler/interpreter per language (Julia, Go, Node, Python with native deps), and running each project's actual test suite — well beyond an embedded pure-language interpreter; effectively requires full native language toolchains and real network egress or a very large pre-baked repo mirror.
quality_notes: High-quality, realistic, hard-to-hack tasks: grading reruns the real project test suite against a hidden test patch, so passing generally requires an actually correct fix. Main risk is environment flakiness (network-dependent clone/build steps, version-pinned toolchains) rather than reward hacking. No leaked solution or visible answer at agent time was found in the sampled tasks.

template_description: Competitive-programming problems (harvested from Codeforces/AtCoder/DMOJ-style sources) requiring a single Python solution file at /app/solution.py that reads from stdin and writes to stdout. The verifier is a pytest file (test_state.py) that feeds each bundled sample input to the agent's script via subprocess and asserts the stripped output lines exactly match the bundled expected output. Only the problem statement's own sample IO (typically exactly one case) ships in tests/test_data.json — no larger hidden test set was found in the sampled tasks. Dockerfile is a minimal Ubuntu image with python3/pip3/venv and generic CLI tools; nothing beyond a stock Python interpreter is actually required. A solution/solve.sh oracle exists per task but is not part of the agent's build context.
unlock_notes: Agent side only needs a real Python interpreter with basic stdlib (sys, math, itertools, collections) — no third-party packages observed — so python_interp alone would make the agent side runnable; the verifier itself is a portable pytest/subprocess harness.
quality_notes: Problems themselves are genuine, varied-difficulty competitive-programming tasks (well_defined 3-4), but grading against only a single sample test case is a structural weakness: several problems have small output spaces (Yes/No, single-letter winner) or a single fixed numeric/graph answer, so blind or overfit guesses have a non-trivial chance of scoring full reward without a general solution. One sampled task (graph construction) also has a spec/verifier mismatch: the instruction says any valid construction is accepted, but the verifier does an exact line match against one specific sample answer.

template_description: Standalone competition-style math word problems where the agent must reason to a final answer and write it (ideally as \boxed{...}) to /app/answer.txt. The verifier (tests/verifier.py) is a generic 'typed boxed-math' grader shared across the whole family: it extracts the last \boxed{} expression (or a labeled 'answer is ...' line), normalizes it, and compares it against tests/verifier_data.json's expected_answer using sympy-based equivalence for the declared answer_type (scalar, equation, interval, set, etc.). Dockerfile is python:3.11-slim with sympy and an ANTLR runtime for LaTeX parsing; no code needs to run beyond the agent's own reasoning and the verifier's parser. No solution files were required to be written by the agent — solution/solve.sh only exists as the oracle reference used to generate the expected answer.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text output (text_only); nothing here needs shell tools beyond writing a file, so it already fits shellsim's echo/heredoc capabilities. The verifier's sympy-based comparison runs host-side against the produced text, not inside the sandbox.
quality_notes: Generally well-specified problems with a single scalar/expression answer and a robust host-side symbolic-equivalence checker, so hack risk is low for tasks with large or hard-to-guess answer spaces. A few sampled problems have small or binary answer spaces (e.g. a game-winner 'A'/'B' or a bounded integer sum a+b) where a lucky guess has meaningful odds of matching; the 'equation' answer_type is also more fragile since many algebraically different but valid equations could satisfy the same word problem while only one canonical form is scored as correct.

template_description: Each task is a single short-answer logic/math puzzle (alphabetical sorting, basic arithmetic, prime counting, advanced geometry, blicket-style causal 'acre' inference) drawn from a generic puzzle-generator dataset, rendered into a fixed instruction template asking the agent to write one line to /app/answer.txt. The verifier (tests/compare_answer.py, identical across the family) reads /tests/gold.json, normalizes both gold and agent answers per an answer_type tag (choice/exact/number/coords/ordered_list), and does a deterministic comparison with small numeric tolerance; tests/test_state.py is a trivial pytest that just re-checks reward.txt equals 1. The agent needs nothing beyond writing a text file (text_only); it never needs a real interpreter. tests/gold.json and solution/solve.sh (an oracle that just prints the gold answer) exist in the task directory but are not COPYed into the Dockerfile, so they are not visible to the agent inside the running container, only mounted for the verifier — no leak observed. The Dockerfile installs python3 + pytest solely to run the verifier script and test_state.py; it is not needed by the agent at all.
unlock_notes: Already runnable: the agent only needs to `echo` or `printf` a short computed answer into a file. No parsing/interpreter dependency for the agent side; verifier is host-side python which is fine.
quality_notes: Very low task difficulty and low novelty — one-shot Q&A puzzles with a single-line deterministic answer, mostly trivial (sorting/arithmetic) though a few (acre blicket inference, advanced_geometry) require actual multi-step reasoning. Spec is crisp and matches the verifier well. Main hack risk is a small answer space for choice-type puzzles (acre: on/off/undetermined, 1-in-3 blind guess) and short ordered-lists (3-4 words) that could occasionally be guessed; number/geometry answers are not guessable. No leaked gold data observed in the agent-visible files.

template_description: Competitive-programming tasks pulled from Codeforces (via the CodeElo benchmark), each giving the full problem statement plus 1-3 worked examples and asking the agent to write /app/solution.py, solution.cpp, or Solution.java. tests/test.sh locates and (if needed) compiles the submission, then for each of 20 shipped tests/inputs/input_N.txt runs it with a 30s timeout and compares stdout to tests/outputs/output_N.txt via tests/judge.py, which does an exact-match compare unless a tests/checker.py special judge is present (rare in this batch; codeelo-0113 has none). Reward is 1 only if every test passes. The agent needs a real interpreter/compiler (python3, g++, or javac) which the Dockerfile installs; the pip install of numpy/scipy/sympy/networkx is convenience/unused by most solutions. Test inputs/outputs are visible to the agent under /tests at agent time (not just at verify time), so an agent could in principle special-case on exact input text, though genuinely solving still requires real logic since inputs vary and there is no held-out set beyond the visible 20.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Python (or C++) interpreter capable of running arbitrary competitive-programming code (loops, recursion, data structures, math, bitwise ops); shellsim's python shim cannot run real scripts. A python_interp extension with stdlib (sys, math, itertools, heapq, bisect) would unlock most of these; the C++ solutions would additionally need compiled_lang, which is out of scope.
quality_notes: Interesting and well-specified — these are real, verbatim Codeforces problems with genuine algorithmic content (data structures, geometry, game theory) at varied difficulty (ratings 0-12 in this sample, though several show rating 0/empty tags due to missing metadata). Hack risk is low because full test cases must pass exactly, but the sampled codeelo-0113 is defective: the problem is an *interactive* Codeforces problem (adaptive judge responses depend on the contestant's queries), yet the verifier replays a static, pre-recorded input file non-interactively and diffs stdout — this cannot correctly grade a true interactive solution and is a template-level defect for any interactive problem pulled into this dataset.

template_description: Same competitive-programming template as laion__codeelo-v2 (verbatim Codeforces problem statement, write /app/solution.{py,cpp,java}, tests/test.sh byte-identical between the two sources), pulled from a different/larger Codeforces scrape (v3). 20 input/output pairs per task under tests/inputs and tests/outputs, exact-match via tests/judge.py, with tests/checker.py present for problems that have multiple valid outputs (e.g. constructive problems needing a special judge, seen in codeforces-06382 and codeforces-06386). Agent needs a real interpreter/compiler; Dockerfile is identical to codeelo-v2's. Test data is visible to the agent at agent time.
unlock_notes: Same as codeelo-v2: needs a real Python/C++ runtime with stdlib support for arbitrary algorithmic code; a pure python_interp extension unlocks the Python-solution path.
quality_notes: Generally solid, well-specified real CF problems spanning strings, graphs (MST), data structures, and game theory, with special-judge checkers correctly used for problems with multiple valid answers. One clear defect found: codeforces-06393 and codeforces-06393_copy1 are byte-identical duplicates of the same problem under different task ids, inflating the apparent dataset size without adding variety. No other reward-hacking issues observed beyond the generic risk that visible test cases could be pattern-matched rather than genuinely solved.

template_description: BugsInPy-derived bug-fixing tasks: each isolates a single buggy method from a real project (mostly pandas, one scrapy in this batch) into a small self-contained /app/solution.py (a miniature reimplementation with just the classes/functions needed, not the full library), and asks the agent to fix it in place (it is a symlink to /setup_files/solution.py). tests/test.sh hashes the submitted file against tests/baseline_sha256.txt to reject unmodified submissions, py_compiles and imports it, then runs pytest against /tests/test_solution.py with a 300s timeout, scoring 1 only if pytest reports passed>0 and no failures; infra errors (import crash, zero tests collected) exit nonzero rather than scoring 0, distinguishing bug-not-fixed from broken harness. The agent needs a real Python interpreter and pytest. Critically, /setup_files/test_solution.py is explicitly documented in instruction.md as visible to the agent and is byte-identical to /tests/test_solution.py, the actual grading file — so the full grading assertions are known in advance by design.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Python interpreter plus pytest (a pure-Python package) to both import the miniature solution module and run the exact grading test file; the miniature reimplementations avoid needing the real pandas/scrapy/numpy, so python_interp + pytest (python_pure_pkgs) should suffice without native deps.
quality_notes: Moderately interesting, well-scoped single-method bug fixes with crisp, matching specs (well_defined ~4-5) grounded in real upstream pandas/scrapy commits. Hack risk is low-moderate: since the exact test file is deliberately shown to the agent, there is no genuine hidden-test protection — a policy could in principle special-case behavior to satisfy the literal assertions without a general fix, though the miniature classes are small enough that this is close to actually fixing the bug. No leaked oracle solution or writable reward file was found; the sha256-baseline check meaningfully blocks no-op submissions. Minor defects: a few tasks (e.g. bugsinpy-0334, bugsinpy-0333) bundle two related upstream test targets into one task, slightly widening scope, and bugsinpy-0350's metadata.json records unittest-style test_command strings that don't reflect the verifier's actual pytest invocation.

template_description: Each task is an LLM-paraphrased retelling of the same CodeNet 'Christmas Countdown' problem: read an integer day D from stdin and print a phrase like 'Christmas Eve Eve' depending on D, implemented at /app/solution.py in a plain python:3.12-slim image. The verifier runs the agent's solution.py against 2-3 hidden stdin/stdout fixture pairs generated from a single fixed oracle one-liner (`print(-int(input('Christmas'))%5*' Eve')`, base64-encoded identically in every solution/solve.sh) and requires all fixtures to whitespace-match, requiring at least 2 checks to pass. Tests/inputs and solve.sh are not copied into the agent's image, so the oracle and hidden cases are not visible at agent time. The Dockerfile only provides a bare Python interpreter, which is essential since the agent must actually execute stdin-reading Python.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Python interpreter that can execute a file with input()/int()/modulo/string-multiplication and print with a trailing newline; shellsim's python shim only handles -c one-liners and cannot run solution.py as invoked by the verifier (`python3 /app/solution.py < input`).
quality_notes: Trivial, boilerplate-generated task family (interesting=1) with a tiny discrete input domain that invites hardcoding. More seriously, in 6 of the 11 variants the paraphrased instructions specify a different behavior for D outside 22-25 (no output, 'No holiday', 'No celebration', 'Not a Christmas related day', or 'print nothing') while the hidden test fixtures still use the underlying oracle's mod-5 wraparound formula and expect strings like 'Christmas Eve Eve Eve Eve' for e.g. D=21 or D=26 — a genuine spec/verifier mismatch that would penalize an agent that correctly follows the written instructions.

template_description: CrossCodeEval-style line-completion tasks: the instruction shows a real open-source C# file truncated mid-declaration and asks the agent to write only the short (1-3 line) continuation to /app/solution.txt, with extensive guidance (and a pre-installed `write_solution` helper) to avoid bash-quoting failures on C# punctuation. The Dockerfile is python:3.10-slim with git and pytest installed (pytest is unused cruft for this task) plus the write_solution.sh helper script. The verifier (tests/test.sh) is a 4-tier forgiving grader: exact match after whitespace normalization, agent-output-starts-with-gold, first-identifier-token match, or a 0.25 rubber-stamp reward for any non-empty <=400-character fragment containing a C# identifier. The gold reference lives only in tests/solution.txt and solution/solution.txt, neither of which is copied into the agent's image.
unlock_notes: The agent side is pure shell (single-quoted string, printf/echo redirection); shellsim's coreutils and shell already cover the write_solution helper and printf-based fallback. The verifier is bash+diff/awk/grep only and would run fine against shellsim's VFS output file.
quality_notes: Genuinely interesting underlying skill (cross-file code completion needing real repo context the snippet doesn't fully provide), but the verifier as built is close to gameable: tier 3 (leading-identifier-only) and especially tier 4 (any short C#-shaped text) let a policy collect nonzero, often full, reward without producing a correct completion, so measured pass rates likely overstate real completion accuracy. No leaked solution and no ambiguity in the instructions themselves.

template_description: Same CrossCodeEval line-completion family as the csharp-v4/python-v2 sources but an earlier template revision applied to real Java source files: the agent sees a truncated Java file and must write the short continuation to /app/solution.txt. Unlike the v4/v2 templates, this verifier is strict: tests/test.sh does a single whitespace-normalized diff between /app/solution.txt and tests/expected.txt with no forgiving tiers, no partial credit, and no write_solution helper mentioned in the instructions. The Dockerfile installs git and pytest even though nothing in the actual grading path uses them (tests/test_solution.py is a leftover pytest file for a different, module-import-based task shape that test.sh never invokes). The gold answer (solution/solution_snippet.txt, copied by solve.sh into expected.txt) is not present in the agent's image.
unlock_notes: Agent only needs to write a text fragment via printf/echo to a file; shellsim's coreutils suffice. The verifier is bash + sed/awk/diff, directly portable against shellsim's VFS.
quality_notes: More honestly graded than its v2/v4 siblings since it has no leading-identifier or non-empty rubber-stamp fallback, so hack risk is lower; correctness still hinges on cross-file context the agent doesn't have, making some fragments essentially unguessable, which limits interestingness as a training signal without artificially favoring long attempts. The stray, unused tests/test_solution.py is a minor defect (dead code / template drift) rather than something exploitable.

template_description: CrossCodeEval line-completion tasks on real Python source files, structurally identical to the crosscodeeval-csharp-v4 family (write_solution helper, python:3.10-slim + git + pytest image, same 4-tier forgiving grader: exact match, startswith, leading-identifier, and a 0.25 rubber-stamp for any short non-empty Python-shaped fragment). The gold fragment (tests/solution.txt) and an unused tests/test_state.py are present in the tests/ fixture but not baked into the agent's image. test.sh always exits 0 once past the missing-file checks, regardless of computed reward, so grading must read /logs/verifier/reward.txt rather than the exit status.
unlock_notes: Agent side is a single printf/write_solution shell invocation, fully within shellsim's coreutils/shell support. Verifier is bash/sed/awk/grep/diff text comparison against a VFS file, directly portable.
quality_notes: Same interesting-but-gameable profile as crosscodeeval-csharp-v4: real cross-file completions are a legitimate hard skill, but tiers 3-4 of the verifier award reward for plausible-looking short snippets without verifying real correctness, inflating apparent success. The exit-code-vs-reward-file mismatch in test.sh is a latent integration defect for any harness that trusts the shell exit status.

template_description: Each task presents a real-world TypeScript file truncated mid-declaration and asks the agent to write the short (1-3 line) continuation to /app/solution.txt using a pre-installed write_solution shell helper. The verifier normalises whitespace and does an exact diff against a hidden gold continuation in /tests/solution.txt, falling back to an agent-startswith-gold check, then a leading-identifier match, then a blanket 0.25 partial credit for any short non-empty fragment resembling code. Only bash and the helper script are needed at agent runtime; no interpreter or compiler is exercised. tests/ and solution/ (which holds the same gold text, not full context) are not copied into the image, so the gold answer is not visible to the agent, but the forgiving scoring tiers substantially weaken the signal.
unlock_notes: Already fully runnable: shell, printf/echo, and a trivial helper script are all shellsim supports today.
quality_notes: Low interest (boilerplate line-completion, not a real coding task) and the verifier's tier-3/tier-4 forgiveness makes it highly hackable -- a policy emitting any short plausible-looking TypeScript token stream can reliably earn partial credit and often full credit via the leading-identifier tier without actually solving the completion. Recommend either tightening the verifier (drop tier 4, require closer similarity) or discounting this family's reward as a noisy signal.

template_description: Each task gives a fully spelled-out GitHub Actions workflow spec (workflow name, triggers, required job ids/runners, required action names in order) and asks the agent to write it to /app/.github/workflows/main.yml. The verifier runs yamllint in a relaxed mode (only hard syntax errors fail) and then a Python structural comparator (compare_workflows.py) that scores fractional coverage of the reference's job ids and 'uses' action names against permissive thresholds (>=70% job coverage, >=50% action coverage, or >=50% single-job action coverage). The agent only needs a shell and a text editor equivalent; the verifier needs Python with PyYAML/yamllint. No solution files are present -- the reference workflow is only under tests/, mounted at verify time.
unlock_notes: Agent side needs only file writes (heredoc/printf to a path); shellsim already supports this. Verifier itself needs a real Python (PyYAML, yamllint) but that runs host-side against the produced file, not inside the sandboxed agent, so it doesn't gate shellsim feasibility.
quality_notes: Low-to-moderate interest -- since the instruction spells out the exact jobs/runners/actions required, the task is largely transcription rather than genuine reasoning. Well-specified and low hack risk: coverage thresholds are generous but the required content is given directly, so there's little room to game beyond correctly copying the spec into valid YAML.

template_description: Each task supplies one JUnit 5 test method (verbatim, extracted from a real open-source repository via the methods2test dataset) and asks the agent to implement whatever Java classes/methods under /app/src/main/java/ are needed for that single test to compile and pass under `mvn test`. The verifier stages the test class into the Maven project, runs mvn test, and parses Surefire XML reports to require at least one passing TestSolution test case with zero failures/errors/skips. The agent needs a real JDK and Maven (a full compiled-language toolchain); tests/pom.xml and the test file are visible but read-only, and solution/ (present in some tasks) holds only partial signature stubs, not a working implementation.
unlock_notes: Requires a real JVM plus javac/maven dependency resolution and, in several tasks, real multi-threaded timing (Thread.sleep, background verticle deployment) -- effectively unreachable without full compiled-language support, which the spec treats as likely infeasible.
quality_notes: Highly variable difficulty and specification quality: some tasks (e.g. ErrorHandler stack-trace formatting) are self-contained and fair, but many require reconstructing an entire undocumented framework (Vert.x-style ClusterStarter/WatchDog/DukesVerticle/Config classes) from a single test call sequence with no source access -- effectively unsolvable except by guessing, and several of those tests carry no real assertions, so a trivial no-throw stub can pass. Recommend filtering out tasks whose required symbol set implies a non-trivial framework not derivable from the test alone.

template_description: Each task presents a real, fully self-contained JUnit test (drawn from Nemotron-generated JUnit examples, here a Mockito spy-vs-mock demo) and asks the agent to build a runnable Maven project around it under /app/, including the correct test-framework dependencies (junit4/junit5/testng, plus optional mockito/hamcrest/etc.) in pom.xml. The verifier's test.sh always overwrites whatever the agent placed at the test's target path with its own canonical copy of tests/TestSolution.java (keyed by tests/test_meta.json), then patches missing dependencies into pom.xml from a fixed catalog, and finally runs `mvn test` and checks Surefire XML for an all-passing report. The agent needs a JDK+Maven toolchain; the test content itself is never actually agent-authored despite the instruction asking for it.
unlock_notes: Needs a real JVM and Maven dependency resolution (download/cache junit/mockito jars) to compile and run the staged test; no Python-only workaround exists.
quality_notes: Very low interest (mostly transcribing a pom.xml dependency list) and low hack risk given the test file is verifier-controlled, but there is a real spec/verifier mismatch: the instruction tells the agent to write the exact test file itself, while the verifier silently discards and replaces that file, making that portion of the instructed work moot busywork.

template_description: Each task hands the agent a Python 'scaffold' file (setup_files/starter.py) full of classes/functions whose bodies raise NotImplementedError, plus prose in instruction.md restating the docstrings/behavior in more detail; the agent must write a working implementation at /app/<package>/<module>.py. The verifier (tests/test_scaffold.py, identical to setup_files/test_scaffold.py so the agent can read the exact hidden test) is run with pytest inside the container and reward.txt is 1 iff pytest exits 0. Domains vary per task (toy lattice geometry, use-case/auth framework, log-panel CLI, singleton access tokens, mock cluster orchestration, form-filling bot, etc.) but the structure and Docker image (python:3.11-slim-bookworm with numpy/pandas/scipy/etc. preinstalled) are constant. The exact test file is visible to the agent under /setup_files before submission, so this is closer to a spec-complete code-gen exercise than a black-box test.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Python interpreter with class/dict/exception support and pytest; most tasks are pure-stdlib logic so python_interp + python_pure_pkgs (for pytest) would suffice without numpy in most cases, though the Docker image pre-installs numpy/pandas/etc. which some (unseen) tasks might use.
quality_notes: Well-specified, verifiable, and non-trivial code-gen tasks; interest and difficulty are middling (single-file, few dozen lines). Low hack risk since the visible test is a real pytest suite exercising actual behavior, not a keyword/exit-code check, though the agent could in principle write implementations narrowly tailored to the exact literal test cases (e.g., hardcode expected floats) since the test file is fully visible pre-solve.

template_description: Each task presents an LLM-authored instruction.md describing some C++ class/function to implement in /app, and a hidden acceptance test at tests/test_solution.cpp (also visible at /setup_files/test_solution.cpp) that test.sh compiles with g++/CMake/ctest and links against gtest/doctest/catch2/boost-test depending on sniffed includes. In every sampled task (10/10), the actual test_solution.cpp is a verbatim excerpt from an unrelated real open-source project (LLVM, Conduit, fb303/thrift, Chromium, microratchet, NNabla, Intel compute-runtime, TrustWallet, Mesos, Valhalla, ROS2) that has nothing to do with the instruction's described class/function, and pulls in headers/libraries that are not installed in the gcc:13 image (which only has cmake/libgtest-dev/doctest/boost-test/catch2). Compilation therefore fails unconditionally regardless of what the agent writes, so reward.txt is always 0. The Dockerfile install is generic C++ tooling and is not itself the problem; the problem is the instruction/test mismatch, apparently caused by a pipeline that generated instructions from one source snippet and sampled the paired test from a different, unrelated snippet.
unlock_notes: Irrelevant -- even a full C++ compiler+toolchain would not make these solvable, since the required headers/libraries (mesos, fb303, conduit, opencl compute-runtime, trustwallet, valhalla, ros2, nbla) are absent from the image and the tasks are unrelated to the instructions; this family should be excluded rather than unlocked.
quality_notes: Systemically broken: in every one of 10 sampled tasks the hidden test file is an unrelated real-world snippet mismatched to the instruction and depends on libraries never installed, making the tasks unsolvable as configured (reward is always 0 for any submission). Not a hack-risk issue -- there is no known way to pass these tasks at all. This entire generated split should likely be discarded or regenerated with correct instruction/test pairing.

template_description: Despite the 'dockerfile' name, each task's instruction.md asks the agent to build a complete small service/CLI/utility from scratch under /app in a language of the task's choosing (Go, Python, Node.js, Java+Node) -- servers, exporters, converters, REST APIs. All tasks share one generic Dockerfile (ubuntu:24.04 with a broad toolchain: gcc/g++, golang-go, nodejs/npm, openjdk-17, php, python3+pip, ruby, rustc/cargo, sqlite3, maven, etc.), so the Dockerfile itself carries no task-specific setup. tests/test_impl.sh is a real, detailed bash script (invoked by test.sh which only guarantees reward.txt is written) that builds/starts the agent's program, drives it with curl/CLI calls, and checks status codes and response substrings/counts against expected behavior; several tasks require the agent's server to run standalone (long_process) and be probed over HTTP. In multiple sampled tasks the instruction falsely claims a specific dependency is 'installed' (wkhtmltoimage+imgkit, the zof OpenFlow library, a running Solr instance, Java 8) when the shared Dockerfile provides none of it, making those specific tasks likely unsolvable without agent-initiated installs of uncertain feasibility.
unlock_notes: Nearly every task needs a real compiler/interpreter (Go, Node, Java, or Python with third-party libs) plus the ability to start a long-running server process and have it answer real HTTP requests from a driver script -- this requires long_process and net_service beyond just an embedded interpreter; a subset that is pure Python stdlib CLI logic without a server (e.g. delivery-record summarizer) could work with python_interp alone.
quality_notes: Individually well-specified with concrete, testable behavior (status codes, JSON shapes, retention counts) and a real functional test harness rather than a trivial exit-code or keyword check, but roughly 2-3 of 11 sampled tasks specify a dependency (Solr server, zof, wkhtmltoimage) as already installed when the shared generic Dockerfile provides none of it, making those instances effectively unsolvable; the rest look legitimate and moderately interesting.

template_description: Each task extracts one real Go function/struct from an open-source project (with its original license header intact) and asks the agent to reimplement it under /app in a specific declared package name, matching the exact hidden unit test (tests/solution_test.go), which -- unlike the stack-cpp-v4 source -- genuinely corresponds to the instruction in every sampled task. test.sh runs `go mod init`, copies the hidden test file in, runs `go mod tidy`/`go get` to resolve any third-party imports (testify etc.), then `go test -v ./...`, with reward 1 iff exit code 0. The test file is not shown to the agent ahead of time (only described via instruction.md), so this is closer to a black-box TDD task than the scaffold-v3 or stack-cpp-v4 sources. The Dockerfile is minimal (golang:1.21 + git/bash) and sufficient for these self-contained standard-library-heavy tasks.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Go toolchain (go build/go test, go.mod resolution, and for some tasks third-party modules like testify via network go get); no Go interpreter is listed as a plausible shellsim extension so this family is effectively out of reach short of adding a full compiled-language runtime.
quality_notes: Generally well-defined, realistic reimplementation tasks (TLS listener setup, backup rotation, path validation) with a real hidden test as the oracle, so hack risk is low. One sampled task (stack-go-5937) has a critical verifier defect: the hidden test file is gated by `// +build windows`, so it is excluded entirely when compiled on the Linux verification image, making `go test ./...` report 'no test files' and pass with reward 1 regardless of whether the agent implements anything -- a genuine reward-hackable/vacuous verifier. Another (stack-go-2704) has an instruction/test signature mismatch: the prose specifies a `(*tls.Config, error)` return, but the real test uses the return value as a net.Listener.

template_description: Each task asks the agent to implement a JavaScript/CommonJS module under /app/ matching a real-world Jest/Jasmine spec scraped from GitHub (The Stack), staged into the image as tests/test_solution.js. test.sh copies the test file into /app/tests/ and runs `npx jest ... --config jest.config.js`, gating a binary reward.txt on the process exit code. Whether the agent's code is actually exercised varies per task: some specs `require()` the agent's file or spawn it as a child process (legitimate), while several specs are self-contained (define their own reference implementations inline and never import /app's code, or rely on jest-native globals) so they pass regardless of what the agent writes. The Dockerfile is shared across the whole source and globally npm-installs dozens of packages (jest, mocha, chai, sinon, express, mongoose, etc.) to cover the union of all tasks' possible dependencies, most of which are irrelevant to any single task and only a few of which (jest itself) are essential.
unlock_notes: Needs a real (or emulated) Node.js runtime plus npm-installed CommonJS packages (varies per task: express, chai/chai-http, guzzle-like HTTP stacks are PHP not JS here, jest itself, occasionally TypeScript). A pure embedded JS interpreter without npm/module resolution would not suffice for the tasks that require Express servers or child_process spawning of CLI scripts.
quality_notes: Highly uneven quality: several tasks (stack-jest-0388, 0386, 0403) have verifiers that never actually test the agent's implementation (self-contained oracle specs or reliance on jest's built-in `expect`), making them free passes / interesting=2 boilerplate. Others (0393, 0387) use undefined matchers (Jasmine's toBePlaying/spyOn, jest-extended's toBeFalse/toBeTrue) that are not available in the plain-Jest Docker environment, so the suite likely cannot pass at all regardless of the agent — a verifier bug, not an agent-solvable task. The genuinely well-formed tasks (0392 CLI validator, 0380 UniqueQueue, 0383 Contentful normalize) are reasonable small unit-implementation exercises with concrete, checkable behavior.

template_description: Each task asks the agent to implement Java source files under /app/ (in a specific package) that make a real, GitHub-scraped JUnit test file (staged only at /tests/, never copied into /app at agent time) compile and pass. The instructions are auto-generated 'test contracts' listing the well-known imports, the classes/interfaces the test references, and the methods called on them with their arities, extracted mechanically from the hidden test source — the agent never sees the actual test assertions or expected values, only this reflection-style summary. The verifier (test.sh) either runs `mvn test` if a pom.xml exists, or otherwise javac-compiles all discovered .java files under /app together with the hidden test file, links against a bundled JUnit Platform Console Standalone jar, executes it, and parses the human-readable summary counts ("N tests found", "N tests failed", etc.) via awk, requiring found>0 and zero failures/aborts/container-failures before setting reward=1. Tests are not visible or editable by the agent (compiled and injected from /tests/ only at verify time), and no solution files are shipped, so the leaked-answer/overwritable-test hack vectors common elsewhere are largely absent. The Dockerfile (eclipse-temurin:17-jdk + maven + curl'd JUnit console jar) is minimal and essential — nothing extraneous is installed.
unlock_notes: Requires a real JDK (javac + java, optionally Maven) — shellsim explicitly treats compiled-language execution as likely infeasible. There is no interpreter shortcut; the tasks fundamentally need to compile and run bytecode against the JUnit Platform.
quality_notes: Consistent, well-engineered verifier design across the sampled tasks (0946, 0750, 9488, 0918, 2331, 8822, 2549, 0661, 4567, 0046, 1084) — genuinely blind tests, strict pass/fail gating, no leaked oracle. The main weakness is that the *instruction* itself is only an auto-extracted reflection summary (symbol names + call arities), not real behavioral prose, so several tasks (SerializableFreezer, Test118's Production109-118 getters) are underspecified for an agent that hasn't seen the original real-world source project; task difficulty and well-definedness vary a lot by how self-evident the class name/API is (a Counter or Profession POJO is obvious; a ServiceLoader-based EventClientTests or a semantic 'freezer' is not). No solution/test leakage found; classpath-dependency risk (fcrepo/javax.ws.rs jars, Doctrine, etc. potentially missing) is the main latent defect risk though not confirmed broken.

template_description: Tasks ask the agent to implement one or a few PHP classes/interfaces under /app/ (with specified namespaces and PSR-4 paths), extracted from real GitHub PHP projects (phpMyAdmin, MathPHP, contentful, various small libraries), described in reasonably detailed prose instructions rather than an auto-extracted symbol list. The verifier (test.sh) uses tests/discover_tests.php to find the PHPUnit test class name(s) declared in the hidden TestSolution.php, copies that file to /tmp/<class>.php per discovered class, and runs `phpunit --bootstrap /app/autoload.php` against it, tolerating only specific 'missing class' PHPUnit errors that are pre-listed in tests/allowed_missing_classes.txt (an explicit allowance for optional/stub dependencies) and otherwise requiring a clean pass with tests actually executed. Tests are not staged into /app and are not visible to the agent beforehand. The Dockerfile (php:8.2-cli + composer + a directly-downloaded phpunit-10.5.58.phar + a generated PSR-4-style autoload.php) is minimal and essential.
unlock_notes: Needs a real PHP interpreter with PHPUnit 10 to run the hidden test class and a working spl_autoload_register-based class loader; shellsim currently has no PHP support at all (not in the listed coreutils/interpreter set), so this is effectively a new 'php_interp' capability outside the existing extension taxonomy — closest match is other_lang_interp.
quality_notes: This is the most carefully engineered PHP family reviewed: instructions are detailed and mostly self-contained (unlike the auto-extracted junit contracts), the allowed_missing_classes.txt mechanism is a thoughtful way to tolerate legitimately-optional symbols without leaking pass/fail on unrelated grounds, and hidden tests prevent the agent from reading or editing the oracle. Task difficulty is generally small-to-medium (single value objects or small utility classes) and well within a bounded scope, unlike the sibling php-v2-v8 source. No solution leakage observed; main residual risk is composer-dependency availability for any task whose described API type-hints a third-party class (not seen in this sampled trio, but plausible generally).

template_description: Like php-large-v9, tasks ask the agent to implement PHP classes/interfaces under /app/ from real GitHub projects (Laravel, Aimeos, OroCRM, Hashids, Contentstack, a Slim-based framework, etc.), but scope varies far more wildly — from a single trivial value object up to reimplementing most of Laravel's cross-dialect SQL query builder. The verifier is a heavier bootstrap-shim variant of the php-large-v9 pattern: it generates a phpunit_bootstrap.php that class_aliases PHPUnit's namespaced TestCase to legacy PHPUnit_Framework_TestCase and a Tests\TestCase stub, pre-includes the hidden /tests/TestSolution.php, and aliases whatever TestCase subclass it declares to the literal name 'TestSolution' so PHPUnit 10's filename-must-match-classname rule is satisfied; it then runs `phpunit --fail-on-skipped` against a generated phpunit.xml pointing at that one file and greps the summary line for a clean 'OK (N tests...)' or zero Failures/Errors. Hidden tests are not visible to the agent. The Dockerfile (php:8.2-cli + composer + curl'd phpunit-10.phar + generated autoload.php) is minimal and shared across all tasks in the source.
unlock_notes: Same as php-large-v9: needs a real PHP + PHPUnit 10 runtime. Several tasks in this source additionally assume third-party Composer packages (GuzzleHttp, Symfony Security/ExpressionLanguage, Doctrine ManagerRegistry, Slim\App, bcmath/gmp extensions) whose availability is not confirmed in the shared Dockerfile, adding a dependency-provisioning requirement on top of the base PHP interpreter.
quality_notes: Much more scope variance and risk than php-large-v9. Most sampled tasks (0077, 0086, 0102, 0080, 0081, 0100, 0097, 0090, 0107, 0106) are reasonably bounded single/small-class implementations, but stack-php-0085 asks the agent to reimplement essentially all of Illuminate\Database's query builder (four SQL dialects, JSON paths, pagination, aggregates) to satisfy Laravel's own exhaustive DatabaseQueryBuilderTest — a scope mismatch for a bounded RL task, likely near-unsolvable from scratch and almost certainly disproportionate to its sibling tasks' effort level. Several other tasks (0080 Aimeos job controller, 0090 Contentstack SDK, 0097 Qurl HTTP client) depend on real-world framework base classes, test harness fixtures, or network I/O that are referenced but not shown to be present in the visible files, creating meaningful risk of hidden infeasibility through missing scaffolding rather than agent error. No leaked solutions or agent-editable tests observed.

template_description: Each task asks the agent to implement one small, self-contained Python module/function/package (e.g. a range class, list helpers, a CLI, a sieve, a Fibonacci function) under /app so that a fixed pytest suite in /tests passes. The verifier activates a shared venv, installs any captured pip requirements (mostly just pytest, occasionally click/Flask), runs pytest with a junitxml report, and grades pass/fail plus a sanity check that at least one non-skipped test ran. No solution/ directory is ever present, and /tests is only visible at verify time per the instructions (not checked in this batch, but no leaked oracle content was found). The Dockerfile is a generic python:3.12-slim image with a prebuilt venv containing pytest and whatever packages the task declares; the install step is essential when third-party packages (click, Flask) are required.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Python interpreter with stdlib (itertools, os, datetime, enum) at minimum; a few tasks (Flask REST API, click CLI) additionally need python_pure_pkgs for click/Flask plus Flask's test client machinery.
quality_notes: Mostly boilerplate, low-difficulty single-function implementations (interesting 1-3) but generally crisp, testable specs (well_defined 4-5). Several tasks are weakly tested (single test case, or checking only exit_code/substring), making them hackable by trivial stubs or by delegating to a builtin (e.g. sorted() satisfies the 'implement merge sort' task); none had leaked solutions or visible-test editing risk since agent and verifier files are cleanly separated.

template_description: Each task asks the agent to implement a Ruby class/module under /app so a fixed RSpec (occasionally plain Ruby/minitest) spec passes; specs range from tiny utility functions to Rails-controller-shaped code to fragments of large real-world gems (TTY::Prompt, ManageIQ, GoodData, Guard). The verifier requires every *.rb under /app, then runs rspec against /tests/test_solution.rb and writes reward.txt=1 only if rspec exits 0 and at least one example ran; a trailing pytest checks reward.txt==1. Critically, the exact acceptance spec is also copied byte-for-byte into /setup_files/test_solution.rb, which the instructions explicitly tell the agent to read before implementing, so tests are fully visible (not hidden) at agent time. The Dockerfile installs a large generic gem set (rspec, rack, faraday, activesupport, capybara, sidekiq, rubocop, etc.) but not framework-specific gems like Rails or the ManageIQ/GoodData codebases those two tasks actually depend on.
unlock_notes: Needs an embedded Ruby interpreter plus RSpec itself (matchers, custom-matcher DSL, stubbing/doubles) since several tasks build custom RSpec matchers or rely on rspec-mocks; no Python involvement at all.
quality_notes: Quality is inconsistent within this source: several tasks are crisp, self-contained, and moderately interesting (rate limiters, AST builders, board-game merge logic), but two (1363 ManageIQ, 1374 GoodData) require an application framework and live/VCR-recorded API state that is never provided, making them effectively unsolvable, and one (1347) contains a literally unsatisfiable assertion (expect(false).to eq(true)) baked into the spec. Full test visibility via /setup_files somewhat undercuts the 'hidden test' framing but the tests are still fairly hard to game since they check real object behavior rather than trivial exit codes.

template_description: Each task is a competitive-programming problem drawn from the TACO dataset: the agent must write /app/solution.py that reads from stdin and writes to stdout to match expected outputs for a set of pre-generated test cases under /tests/inputs and /tests/outputs. The verifier is a pure shell loop that runs `python3 /app/solution.py < input` for every test file, whitespace-normalizes both actual and expected output, and does exact string comparison, writing reward.txt=1 only if every test passes. A solution/solution.py oracle (typically the original TACO reference answer, sometimes buggy or unrunnable as-is) is present in the extracted archive alongside the task but the Dockerfile never copies it into the built image, so it is not visible to the agent at solve time. The Dockerfile is a bare python:3.10-slim with only pytest installed; no other third-party packages are available, which is a problem for the one task whose oracle solution imports numpy.
