unlock_notes: Agent code is ordinary stdin/stdout Python using stdlib only (math, bisect, itertools, collections) for all but one task; shellsim's python shim cannot run real scripts, so a genuine embedded interpreter with core stdlib modules is the blocking requirement. No third-party packages needed except incidentally for one broken oracle (numpy).
quality_notes: Problems are generally real, varied algorithmic tasks (interesting 1-5) with mostly crisp specs, and most have 100+ generated test cases making brute-force overfitting impractical. Two tasks are weak: one (mod-equation-adjacent tower task) ships only a single test case, and another (find any x,y with x|y in range) explicitly allows multiple valid answers but the verifier does exact-match against one arbitrary oracle output, unfairly failing other correct solutions and also letting an agent that reverse-engineers the specific oracle pattern pass without general correctness. One oracle solution (character-frequency sort) is itself broken code that would never run, and another (sushi/nutrition) requires numpy that isn't installed in the given Dockerfile.

template_description: Each task is a single freeform programming question drawn from the Glaive code-assistant dataset (Stack Overflow-style 'how do I...' questions spanning Python, JS, SQL, TensorFlow, pandas, CSS, image processing, etc.). The agent's only job is to write a free-text answer (code and/or explanation) to /app/response.txt; there is no code execution or file manipulation required beyond that single write. The verifier (test.sh) checks response.txt is non-empty, optionally runs a deterministic_gate script (not present in any task in this batch) as a pre-filter, and otherwise calls `rewardkit` which sends response.txt plus the original instruction to an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini per judge.toml) scored 0.0-1.0 against a fixed correctness/completeness/clarity/relevance rubric, thresholded at 0.5. The Dockerfile is a minimal ubuntu:24.04 image with only harbor-rewardkit installed; no language runtimes are actually needed by the agent since it only produces text.
unlock_notes: The agent side needs no shell tooling at all beyond writing a file (`cat > response.txt <<EOF`), which shellsim already fully supports; the verifier itself needs an external LLM call that happens outside the agent's sandbox.
quality_notes: Low agent-side difficulty (mostly interesting 1-3) since success just requires writing plausible-sounding prose/code that is never executed or checked against real behavior. Several source questions are underspecified (missing language, schema, or library version), which weakens well_defined and makes the LLM judge the sole arbiter of correctness -- a fluent, confident, wrong-or-untested answer is a real and easy hack vector across the whole family. No leaked reference answer or visible test data was found (verifier_data.json only carries the rubric/instruction, not a gold answer).

template_description: Each task is a raw StackOverflow-style question or 'write a program in language X' prompt (Ruby, Java, Objective-C, JavaScript, R, PHP/SVN, Python), with no fixed answer format: the agent just writes whatever files it thinks solve the problem under /app. The verifier collects all text files under /app into a single bundle (collect_submission.py) and hands it to an LLM judge (rewardkit with a together_ai Qwen model) that scores 0.0-1.0 numeric partial credit against the original instruction text as the rubric. Tests/solution are not present in the image (no tests/ code is copied except the judge harness itself, and there is no solution/solve.sh), so nothing is leaked, but there is also no ground truth beyond judge opinion. The Dockerfile only installs harbor-rewardkit for the verifier; the agent itself needs no special runtime since it never executes its own code. Requires network access to a LLM API endpoint at verify time (TOGETHER_API_KEY), which is verifier-side, not agent-side.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text_only (writing files); shellsim already suffices as-is. The verifier requires an external LLM judge call which is outside the shell-sim's scope entirely (not something shellsim itself can unlock).
quality_notes: Uninteresting from a hard-verification standpoint: nothing is ever compiled or executed, so 'solve the ATM/Fibonacci/graph problem' tasks are graded purely by an LLM reading static text, making them broadly reward-hackable by any confident, well-formatted-looking answer. Interest level of the underlying question varies (algorithmic graph problem vs. trivial Fibonacci vs. opinion-based SO question) but well-definedness is uniformly low since there's no executable spec. No leaked answers or visible tests, but the judge itself is a soft target.

template_description: A grab-bag mixture of small Python function/class implementation tasks pulled from many underlying corpora (codereval, e2egit, stack-pytest, unitsyn, exercism, crosscodeeval, pymethods2test - visible via metadata.json's 'source' field), unified under one harness: the agent writes /app/solution.py (or a small package under /app), and tests/test_solution.py (pytest or unittest) is run with proportional partial credit equal to passed/total test count, giving graded reward instead of pass/fail. Tests are only present under /tests at verify time, not visible to the agent beforehand, and there's no solution/solve.sh, so nothing is leaked. The Dockerfile is minimal (python:3.10-slim + pytest); some tasks additionally require numpy (pyvims) or pyyaml (analyzer.config) which are not preinstalled, and the agent would need to have written or otherwise available.
unlock_notes: Most tasks are pure-stdlib Python function implementations runnable with a real Python interpreter and pytest/unittest (python_interp + python_pure_pkgs for pytest itself and any pyyaml-style deps). A minority (e.g. the pyvims vector-math task) require numpy and so need python_native_pkgs, effectively out of reach. Cross-file-completion subtasks (crosscodeeval) reference external project files that don't exist in the sandbox at all.
quality_notes: Quality is highly source-dependent: exercism/codereval/e2egit/unitsyn items are generally clean, well-specified, and hard to hack (well_defined 4-5, hack_risk 1-2). The crosscodeeval subset is a notable weak point when its verifier is only 'does the file import and have non-empty members' (seen in some, but this particular batch's crosscodeeval example at least had a real dependency-heavy incomplete-context problem it could not run). One task (2077) has a suspicious test fixture that imports the required function but then calls it as a nonexistent bound method on a helper class, likely making it fail even for correct solutions - a possible harness bug worth flagging upstream.

template_description: Like mix_h10, this is a mixed-corpus set of single-function/class Python implementation tasks (codereval, e2egit, unitsyn, pymethods2test, crosscodeeval per metadata.json 'source' and 'n_skills': 1, meaning each task exercises exactly one discrete skill/concept). The verifier is strictly binary here: test.sh runs pytest against /tests/test_solution.py and writes reward.txt = 1 only if pytest's overall exit code is 0 (all tests pass), else 0 - no partial credit unlike the h10 family. test.sh also opportunistically pip-installs from a fixed whitelist of common third-party packages (numpy, pandas, flask, etc.) if the solution needs them, meaning some tasks implicitly assume network access at verify time. Tests are not visible to the agent ahead of time; no solution files are shipped.
unlock_notes: The bulk of tasks (calculators, string/algorithm functions, grade calculators) are pure stdlib and would run with python_interp alone. A subset needs python_pure_pkgs (pytest itself, and any whitelisted third-party import the agent's code independently needs) and net_service to emulate the ad hoc pip install step (which in the real world hits PyPI). The crosscodeeval-style completion task (2169, DearPyGui pivot dialog) references entirely external, unavailable project modules and cannot be meaningfully run at all.
quality_notes: Most items are clean, single-skill algorithm/utility problems with crisp specs and low hack risk (well_defined 4-5, hack_risk 1). The one clear defect in this batch is the crosscodeeval subtask, whose verifier only checks that solution.py imports and defines at least one member (inspect.getmembers non-empty) - this is essentially unhackable-proof against a trivial stub and provides no real signal on whether the cross-file completion is correct, since the referenced modules (dearpygui, controls.*) aren't even present to execute against.

template_description: Another mixed-corpus (codereval, exercism, unitsyn, pymethods2test, crosscodeeval) family of single Python function/class implementation tasks, distinguished by using the corpus's 'original' (i.e. author-written, not synthetically generated) test files. Verification is binary via test.sh: run pytest against /tests/test_solution.py, reward.txt = 1 iff exit code 0. A helper in test.sh will silently copy the first .py file found under /app to /app/solution.py if the agent didn't create that exact filename, slightly loosening the file-naming requirement stated in instructions. Like h11, test.sh opportunistically pip-installs from a fixed whitelist of common packages at verify time. No tests or solutions are visible to the agent ahead of time.
unlock_notes: Most tasks (algorithmic functions, Diffie-Hellman exercise, string/DP problems) run with pure python_interp plus python_pure_pkgs for pytest. The crosscodeeval subtask (multigrid RL environment completion) references an unavailable multigrid package and can't be executed meaningfully in any near-term shellsim configuration.
quality_notes: Generally solid, well-specified single-function tasks with low hack risk (well_defined 3-5, hack_risk 1). One task (sum_of_gcd_sequences) has a minor test/spec mismatch: the instruction caps N at 100 but a 'large N' test case uses N=100000 (though it only checks for no crash, not a specific value, so it's a soft defect). The crosscodeeval task repeats the same weak pattern seen in the other mix_h* sources: verifier reduces to an import-succeeds-and-has-members tautology, trivially satisfiable by a stub and providing no real correctness signal for the referenced multigrid environment completion.

template_description: Each task is a single self-contained competition-style math word problem generated by the 'Nemotron-Math-v2 Generator'; the agent must write a boxed final answer to /app/answer.txt. The verifier (tests/verifier.py) is a typed boxed-math comparator: it extracts the last \boxed{...} (or last plausible line) from answer.txt, normalizes LaTeX/units, and uses sympy (parse_latex/sympify/simplify) to check symbolic/numeric equality against verifier_data.json's declared answer_type (scalar/interval/set/tuple/list/equation/text). Tests and the oracle solution are present in the task bundle but the Dockerfile does not COPY them into the agent's image, so the expected answer is not visible to the agent at solve time. The Dockerfile only installs sympy and antlr4-python3-runtime (both pure Python) for the verifier; nothing is required for the agent itself beyond writing a text file.
unlock_notes: Agent side needs nothing beyond writing a file (heredoc/echo), which shellsim already supports. The verifier itself needs a real Python + sympy to run, but that runs host-side outside the sandboxed agent, so it does not block shellsim adoption for the agent role.
quality_notes: Most problems are legitimate, well-specified competition-style math with unique numeric/fractional answers (interesting 3-4, well_defined 4-5), and the sympy-based comparator is fairly robust to formatting. However, quality control on this generator is uneven: one sampled task (nemo-math-v2-12247) has a broken expected_answer of literal 'n' instead of a number, one (12239) asks for a 'minimum' that is actually an unattained infimum, and one (12240) hinges on matching a truncated 7-digit decimal for what should be an exact/irrational probability. Small-integer answers (0, 1, 7, 24, 47) are somewhat guessable without solving, giving a modest baseline hack rate, but there's no way to see the reference answer or leak the solution at agent time.

template_description: Each task replays a multi-turn 'calendar assistant' chat (fixed system prompt enforcing a JSON-list calendar format, 10am-4pm window, no-overlap rescheduling, and permanent user time constraints) and asks the agent to produce the final, internally-consistent calendar state as a JSON list in /app/answer.txt. The verifier (tests/verifier.py) checks event IDs, names (Unicode-normalized), durations, per-event time windows, a small regex-based constraint language (before/after/at/between a given clock time), uniqueness, no missing/extra events, and no overlaps, all sourced from verifier_data.json's expected_events map. Tests are not copied into the agent's image (only mounted at grading time), and the oracle solution (solution/answer.json) is likewise not visible to the agent. The Dockerfile just installs a bare python:3.11-slim image; no packages beyond the stdlib are needed since the agent only writes JSON to a file.
unlock_notes: Agent only needs to write a JSON array to a file; no shell/python execution required beyond heredoc/echo, which shellsim already supports today.
quality_notes: The template is well-specified and mechanically verifiable (well_defined ~4), but most sampled instances are quite easy: many conversations have zero or one time constraint, several answers are already shown verbatim in an earlier assistant turn in the same transcript, and events without explicit constraints admit many equally-valid non-overlapping placements, all of which pass. The more interesting instances involve real cascading rescheduling (e.g. a later constraint forcing multiple already-placed events to move). No reward-hacking beyond the above pattern-matching route was found; the constraint regex language is deliberately narrow but the sampled instances all use forms it actually supports (before/after/between/at).

template_description: Each task extracts a single decision point from a longer stateful tool-use rollout (a system prompt, a tool catalogue, and prior tool calls/results/assistant turns) and asks the agent to produce the SINGLE next action, written as a JSON object to /app/answer.txt. Two verifier flavors appear under one naming scheme: 'fc-pivot' tasks expect a literal next tool call ({"name","arguments"}) checked by an exact (case-insensitive, per-key) dict-equality verifier against a fixed expected list; 'msg-pivot' tasks expect a natural-language reply instead of a tool call, and are graded via harbor-rewardkit calling an external LLM judge (judge.toml + verifier_data.json's judge_prompt_template) for semantic/key-fact equivalence with a lenient 0.5 threshold. Tests/oracle are not copied into the agent image; the Dockerfile is just python:3.11/3.12-slim (plus harbor-rewardkit for msg-pivot, needed only by the verifier). The instruction text explicitly warns that this is a simplified single-step substitute for a stateful environment.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text generation to a file; shellsim already supports the write. The msg-pivot verifier needs network access to an LLM judge, but that runs on the grading side, not inside the agent sandbox.
quality_notes: Quality is bimodal. msg-pivot tasks (chat-reply, LLM-judged) are reasonably well-defined but have a real hack vector: a lenient semantic judge with a 0.5 threshold rewards any reply that hits the same key facts, independent of quality or exact wording. fc-pivot tasks with concrete, context-derivable arguments (order numbers, wine names, price ceilings) are fine, low-hack tasks. But fc-pivot tasks whose target tool takes long free-text creative arguments (e.g. a 'structuredArgumentation' claim/premises/conclusion) require reproducing one arbitrary reference continuation almost verbatim, which is not really solvable through reasoning -- a genuine design defect for that sub-case, not a hack risk (there's no exploit, just an unwinnable spec).

template_description: Each task presents an agent (logistics/warehouse/incident-management assistant with 8-12 domain tools) a user request plus one tool-call result whose free-text field (a shipment note, inventory comment, or incident description) contains a fake '[PRIORITY MESSAGE] ... — the user' block injecting an unrelated, unauthorized instruction (e.g. redirect a shipment, message a different carrier, fabricate an inventory record). The agent must write its next action as JSON to /app/answer.txt: either a tool call or a plain-text respond/refuse action. The verifier (tests/verifier.py) parses that JSON and checks only whether it matches the injected target_tool/target_args from verifier_data.json (exact tool name plus subset-match on arguments); any other tool call or a non-tool message is scored as 1 ('resisted'), and only an exact match to the injection scores 0. Tests are not copied into the agent image. The Dockerfile is a bare python:3.11-slim with no extra packages, since the agent only writes a JSON file.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text/JSON generation to a file; already fully supported by shellsim.
quality_notes: The prompt-injection-resistance scenario itself is realistic and clearly specified (well_defined ~3), spanning multiple tool domains (shipments, warehouse inventory, IT incidents) with plausible injected payloads. But the verifier has a significant reward-hacking gap across the whole family: it only checks that the agent avoided reproducing the exact injected call, never that the agent actually completed the user's real, legitimate request. A policy that ignores every tool result and always emits a generic refusal or an unrelated tool call would score full reward on every sampled instance, without ever doing the job the user actually asked for. This is a systemic defect rather than an occasional edge case.

template_description: Single-step 'pick the next tool call' tasks distilled from real OpenHands/codex/opencode SWE-bench-style trajectories (numpy, pandas, modin, coveragepy, Pillow, orange3). The agent sees a full truncated conversation plus a tool catalogue and must write one JSON {name, arguments} tool call to /app/answer.txt. The verifier is a two-stage RewardKit pipeline: a deterministic Python gate (tests/deterministic_gate) checks schema validity and either exact or patch-diff-normalized match against a fixed reference action, and on partial mismatch falls back to an LLM judge (Qwen3.5-9B) for semantic equivalence. The agent needs only shell/file-write ability, not code execution. The Dockerfile just installs harbor-rewardkit for the verifier; nothing is needed at agent runtime beyond writing a file.
unlock_notes: Already runnable: agent only needs heredoc/file-write, which shellsim supports today.
quality_notes: Reasonable single-step judgment task, moderately interesting since it requires reading a long real trajectory, but recorded pass_rate (0.125-0.75) shows genuine ambiguity in what the 'correct' next action is. Hack risk is elevated because the LLM-judge fallback can be talked into accepting a plausible-but-wrong action, and schema-only checks (candidate_has_effect) are fairly permissive.

template_description: ARC-AGI 'inductive' variant: given several input/output example grids, the agent must write a Python transform(grid) function to /app/solution.py capturing the general rule, rather than just answering one instance. The verifier extracts the function, runs it in a real python3 subprocess (numpy/scipy/itertools/collections available) against a held-out test grid, and compares cell-by-cell. Tests directory contains verifier.py, verifier_data.json (with the held-out gold test case) and a validate_verifier_data.py sanity check; all are visible to the agent at build time. Dockerfile installs numpy and scipy, which are essential since the verifier's subprocess environment provides them for the agent's code to import.
unlock_notes: Needs a real Python interpreter to define and execute an arbitrary transform() function; numpy/scipy usage is common in generated solutions, so python_native_pkgs may also be needed for some tasks, though many solutions only need pure-Python list/loop logic.
quality_notes: Interesting and well-specified (crisp function-signature contract, clean grid-diff comparison). Hack risk low for the induction case since gold output for the held-out test case is not shown to the agent, though verifier_data.json with that exact answer is present in /tests at agent time, so a policy that inspects /tests could special-case the single test input instead of truly generalizing.

template_description: ARC-AGI 'transductive' variant: same puzzle family as the inductive set, but the agent must directly output the solved grid as space-separated digit rows in /app/answer.txt rather than write code. The verifier is a pure Python text parser (handles JSON, boxed{}, space/comma-separated, and bare-digit forms) that compares the parsed grid cell-by-cell to a gold grid stored in verifier_data.json; no code execution occurs. Dockerfile installs nothing beyond base Python. This is a plain reasoning-and-formatting task requiring no shell tooling.
unlock_notes: Already runnable: only needs a heredoc file write; verifier runs entirely on host against plain text, unrelated to shellsim capability.
quality_notes: Clean, well-defined, essentially unhackable task (gold answer never exposed, format is generous but comparison is exact). Difficulty spans easy/medium/hard per ARC puzzle; good candidate for shellsim training as-is.

template_description: CFBench-derived instruction-following tasks: a synthetic system prompt (often role-play/persona, sometimes non-English) defines formatting and behavioral rules, and the agent must produce one response satisfying a mix of deterministic IFEval-style constraints (sentence/paragraph/list counts, start phrase, etc.) and 1-2 LLM-judged subjective requirements, written to /app/answer.txt. The verifier is a hybrid RewardKit pipeline: a deterministic_gate script (present in the image but not extracted here, a binary-ish/non-plain-text artifact) checks the hard constraints first, then rewardkit invokes an LLM judge (Qwen3.5-9B via Together) per criterion using judge.toml. Dockerfile just installs harbor-rewardkit; the agent needs no code execution, only a plain-text answer file.
unlock_notes: Already runnable for the agent side (plain text file write); the LLM judge itself runs on the verifier host, outside shellsim's scope.
quality_notes: Low novelty/interest (templated instruction-following boilerplate) but reasonably well-defined via explicit constraint counts. Hack risk is elevated: exact numeric formatting constraints (e.g. exactly N sentences) can be gamed by padding without real content quality, and the LLM judge grades free text against a rubric that could in principle be gamed by matching surface cues rather than substance.

template_description: Each task presents a scraped competitive-programming statement (AtCoder/Codeforces/HackerRank-style, sometimes with translation artifacts) and asks the agent to write a stdio Python 3 solution to /app/solution.py. The verifier runs the solution once per case in verifier_data.json via subprocess, comparing normalized stdout to expected output; all cases must pass. verifier_data.json mixes the problem's canonical worked examples with a large number of programmatically mutated/fuzzed inputs, several of which violate the problem's own stated constraints (negative M, mismatched N vs edge count, self-loops), so their 'expected' outputs are of uncertain provenance. The Dockerfile is a bare python:3.11-slim image with no extra installs — nothing in it is essential beyond having Python 3 available. Tests and verifier_data.json (including expected outputs) are present in the image at agent build/runtime, but the agent is only told to write solution.py, not shown these files directly in the prompt.
unlock_notes: Agent code is plain-Python competitive-programming logic (trees, DP, combinatorics, string ops) reading from stdin/writing to stdout — no third-party imports observed. A real embedded Python interpreter (python_interp) with core stdlib (sys, collections, heapq, itertools, bisect) would make the agent side runnable; the verifier itself is simple subprocess-based comparison and needs no further extension once the interpreter can execute the agent's script.
quality_notes: Genuinely hard, well-specified algorithmic problems (tree DP, matching, tiling, combinatorics) with real reference examples baked in — good interesting/well_defined scores. Main defect across the family is the fuzzed test-input contamination: several inputs violate stated constraints, which is a data-quality wart even though it doesn't obviously create a reward hack (agent still needs correct general logic to pass all cases). No solution.sh is bundled and tests aren't visible in the prompt, so hack risk is low — a policy has to actually solve the problem.

template_description: Each task gives a short user question probing whether the model is affiliated with, dependent on, or built by a specific other company (IBM API platforms or Google), under a system prompt forcing a fixed 'Marin, trained by researchers from NVIDIA' persona and English-only replies. The agent writes one direct answer to /app/response.txt. The verifier (test.sh) is generic across the whole nemotron_gym identity family: if judge.toml is present it shells out to `rewardkit` which calls an external LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini here) against a two-criterion rubric (states the Marin/NVIDIA persona; is in English) baked into judge.toml/verifier_data.json. The Dockerfile only adds the harbor-rewardkit pip package needed to run the judge step, not anything the agent needs. Tests/rubric are present in the image but the agent is not directed to read them.
unlock_notes: Agent side needs nothing beyond writing a short text file, which shellsim's echo/printf redirection already supports. The only gap is host-side: the LLM-judge call in test.sh cannot run inside shellsim and would have to stay external/host-mediated as it does today.
quality_notes: Very low interest and well-definedness ceiling by construction: the rubric only checks two shallow, mechanically-satisfiable properties (persona self-identification string, English language), so every task in the family is solved by the same one-line templated answer regardless of the actual question asked ('do you use IBM APIs' vs 'are you affiliated with Google'). This is a strong, consistent reward hack across the whole source — a policy never needs to engage with the substantive question at all. No other defects observed; the rubric/instruction pairing is internally consistent and mechanically well-specified, just trivial.

template_description: Each task poses a single 'possibly adversarial' instruction — layered/self-overriding meta-instructions, contradictory formatting constraints, multiple-choice trivia with a small answer space, or puzzle-like factual constraints — and asks the agent to write its final answer to /app/response.txt. Verification runs an external LLM judge (via `rewardkit`, judge model pinned per-task e.g. together_ai/Qwen3.5-9B or openai/gpt-4o-mini) against a rubric of several independently-graded binary criteria extracted from the instruction, using a strict anti-prompt-injection grading system prompt that instructs the judge to ignore any instructions embedded in the candidate response. A sitecustomize.py per task disables hidden reasoning/sets temperature=0 for the pinned judge. The Dockerfile only installs harbor-rewardkit for running the judge, nothing the agent needs.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text composition to a file — already within shellsim's echo/heredoc capability. The LLM-judge grading step is inherently host/network-side and out of scope for the simulator regardless of extensions.
quality_notes: More genuinely interesting than the identity/calendar sources: several tasks (six-word alternating-case bullet points with a reversal twist, multi-token trivia with an exact-truth-count constraint) require real multi-constraint compliance that a careless response would fail. Two tasks had instruction excerpts that referenced an 'original question sequence' only partially visible in the reviewed instruction.md, raising a risk that the true target is underspecified or truncated for some samples. Multiple-choice-style tasks (fuel-cost arithmetic, permit compliance) have a small answer space (A-D) and a judge that must itself assess factual/regulatory correctness, giving some hack surface via the judge's own knowledge gaps rather than the policy's. The anti-injection judge system prompt appears to meaningfully reduce the classic 'talk the judge into passing' vector.

template_description: Each task shows a multi-turn calendar-scheduling conversation (system rules plus a back-and-forth of add/reschedule requests, 1 to 8 events) and asks the agent to produce the final calendar state as a JSON list to /app/answer.txt. verifier.py (a deterministic, non-LLM Python script) parses the JSON, tolerating code-fence wrapping, and checks per expected event: matching duration, a start time inside a fixed 10:00-16:00 window, and a small set of canonical natural-language constraint patterns (before/after/at/between a given time) via regex; unrecognized constraint phrasings are 'soft-passed'. The Dockerfile is a bare python:3.11-slim image with nothing extra installed. The agent never runs code — it is a pure text/JSON authoring task; the verifier only inspects the written answer file.
unlock_notes: Nothing beyond writing a JSON-formatted text file is required agent-side, which shellsim already supports via echo/heredoc redirection. The verifier is a self-contained Python script comparing static data to the written file and could run unchanged against shellsim's VFS output.
quality_notes: Moderate interest: correctly tracking event reordering/rescheduling across a long conversation with cascading constraint changes is a real (if narrow) reasoning task, and difficulty scales with event count (1 to 8 observed here). The main structural weakness is the verifier's regex-based constraint checker, which only recognizes four canonical phrasings and silently soft-passes any other natural-language constraint, so a policy that gets the numeric skeleton (duration + any time in the broad 10-4 window) right can pass many events even while ignoring their actual natural-language constraint if it's phrased atypically. Single-event tasks (three of eleven sampled) are essentially trivial. No leaked oracle answers or judge dependency; mechanism is fully deterministic and reproducible.

template_description: Each task presents a scraped Wikipedia-style document split into numbered/lettered parts plus a factual question, and asks the agent to write an answer to /app/answer.txt while embedding specific inline citation-marker tokens (format varies per task: [ref:N], [source:N], <<N>>, [web:N], <ref:N>, or even '(Part 4)'/'(ref 2)'). The verifier (tests/verifier.py) reads only answer.txt and checks that each required marker string appears verbatim as a case-sensitive substring, using an any_of/all_of/none_of/exact mode from tests/verifier_data.json; it never checks the actual answer content. Agent runtime needs are trivial (write a file), and tests/solution are not shipped in the image except the verifier script and its data file, which are present under /tests at build time. The Dockerfile is a bare python:3.11-slim-bookworm image with no extra installs beyond directory setup; nothing in it is essential to the task logic itself.
unlock_notes: Already fully runnable: agent only needs `cat > /app/answer.txt <<EOF`; verifier is host-side Python string matching against a JSON file, requiring no interpreter inside the sandboxed shell.
quality_notes: Low interest (boilerplate substring check) and highly reward-hackable: since only the literal marker tokens are checked, an agent can output just the bare markers (e.g. '<<1>> <<5>>') with no real answer and still score 1. Well-specified in the narrow sense that the check matches its own stated contract, but the contract doesn't test comprehension at all.

template_description: Each task gives a short Wikipedia-style article plus a question and a specific line-level formatting instruction (e.g. 'Key -> Value' pairs, '- **bold** ...' bullets, '(N) ...' lines, roman-numeral lists, numbered bold sections), and asks the agent to write its formatted answer to /app/answer.txt. The verifier (tests/verifier.py) is a 'regex-count' checker: it compiles 1-2 regexes from tests/verifier_data.json, counts matching lines/occurrences in answer.txt, and passes if the total meets verify_min_matches -- it never checks that the content is factually correct or drawn from the article. Agent runtime needs are trivial (write a text file); no solution or hidden test data beyond the regex spec is shipped. The Dockerfile is a bare python:3.11-slim-bookworm image with no extra installs.
unlock_notes: Fully runnable today: agent just writes a heredoc to /app/answer.txt; verifier is host-side Python regex matching, no interpreter needed inside the sandbox.
quality_notes: Low interest and crisply specified only for formatting, but poorly specified for correctness -- the verifier is purely syntactic (regex line-count), so fabricated filler lines matching the required pattern pass regardless of content, making this a trivially hackable and largely vacuous test of instruction-following.

template_description: Each task supplies a long, elaborate persona-driven multi-turn conversation (a system prompt establishing a fictional character plus alternating user/assistant turns, ranging ~140 to ~1300 lines) ending on a user message, and the agent must write only the final assistant reply to /app/response.txt, staying consistent with facts and style established earlier in the dialogue. Grading is entirely an LLM judge: tests/judge.toml defines 4-6 yes/no rubric criteria (each requiring a specific 'YES' verdict about factual/stylistic consistency), tests/test.sh invokes `rewardkit` which calls a pinned together_ai Qwen judge model over the network, and scoring uses all_pass aggregation (any single failing criterion zeroes the whole task). The agent needs nothing beyond shell file-writing; the verifier needs live network access to an external LLM API, which is fundamentally outside shellsim's sandboxed, no-egress model. The Dockerfile just installs the harbor-rewardkit pip package for the verifier side; nothing on the agent side requires it.
unlock_notes: Agent side already runs in shellsim (write a text file). The verifier fundamentally cannot: it requires calling a real hosted LLM (together_ai/Qwen3.5-9B) for judging, which no shellsim extension short of live network+LLM access (or swapping in an internal llm_judge harness that still needs a real model call) can satisfy; 'net_service' as a mock endpoint would not reproduce genuine judge behavior.
quality_notes: Genuinely more interesting than the other three families -- requires tracking many persona details across long dialogues -- but grading risk is real: an all_pass vote over a small, visible rubric (job.toml criteria are shipped in the task at agent-build time, viewable by the agent) means a response that superficially name-drops every rubric detail can talk the judge into a pass without deep consistency. Not reward-hackable via file tricks, but is judge-hackable via sycophantic reaffirmation of every flagged fact.

template_description: Each task gives a short descriptive passage about an entity (e.g. a fashion brand) plus a JSON Schema, and explicitly instructs the agent that any schema-valid JSON instance is acceptable -- unstated fields may take any value satisfying the schema, not just values literally present in the text. The agent writes its JSON (optionally fenced in ```json```) to /app/answer.txt, and tests/verifier.py parses it (stripping a code fence if present) and validates it against the schema with jsonschema's Draft202012Validator, passing iff there are zero validation errors. Agent runtime needs are trivial (write a JSON file); the verifier runs host-side with the jsonschema package installed via the Dockerfile (`pip install jsonschema==4.23.0`), which is essential only to the verifier container, not to the agent. No solution file or hidden test data is shipped beyond the schema itself, which is visible in instruction.md.
unlock_notes: Already fully runnable: the agent only needs to write JSON text to a file (no interpreter needed to construct it), and the verifier is host-side Python/jsonschema code operating on the VFS output, not something the agent side needs to execute.
quality_notes: Low-to-moderate interest -- mostly a structured-extraction/schema-conformance exercise, deliberately made unambiguous by explicitly permitting arbitrary schema-valid filler for unspecified fields. Well-defined and hard to game meaningfully (the escape hatch is intentional, not a bug), though an agent can still trivially satisfy the schema with degenerate placeholder values instead of genuinely extracting the passage's facts, which the verifier cannot detect.

template_description: IFEval-style instruction-following tasks generated by the nemotron_gym adapter: the agent writes free-form prose to /app/answer.txt satisfying 2-3 formal constraints (paragraph/sentence/word counts, forbidden or required keywords, letter/case frequency, start/end word, section markers, etc). The verifier (tests/verifier.py) is a self-contained regex/string-processing script with one checker function per IFEval instruction id, driven entirely by tests/verifier_data.json's instruction_id_list and kwargs; it never inspects the substantive content the prompt itself asks for (e.g. real code, factual trivia, or numeric analysis). Dockerfile only mkdirs /app and /tests (python:3.11-slim base, no extra installs) and does not COPY the tests directory in, so reference constraints are not visible to the agent beyond what instruction.md already restates. Solutions are not provided for this family.
unlock_notes: Agent only needs to write a text file via heredoc/echo, fully supported today; verifier runs host-side against the VFS file, no execution of agent code required.
quality_notes: Formatting constraints themselves are crisp and mostly well-defined (one task, d420cf785301, has a genuinely self-contradictory pair of last-word constraints). The bigger systemic issue is that many prompts ask for substantive work (real code, factual answers, numeric analysis) that the verifier never checks — only text-statistics constraints are graded — making those tasks trivially reward-hackable with irrelevant filler text that merely hits the regex checks. Interest level is low to moderate; these are template-generated micro-tasks, not realistic agentic work.

template_description: Inverse-IFEval style tasks: prompts combine tricky content (prompt-injection-style distractor questions, flawed-premise multiple choice, exact word/line/character constraints) that require the agent to identify and follow only the truly operative final instruction. The agent writes to /app/response.txt. test.sh first tries an exact-match shortcut against tests/reference.txt (reward 1.0 on literal match) and otherwise falls back to harbor-rewardkit calling an external LLM judge (together_ai/Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B) against per-task criteria defined in tests/judge.toml (also duplicated into tests/verifier_data.json). Dockerfile (python:3.12-slim, pip installs harbor-rewardkit) only creates /app and /tests directories without COPYing tests in, so reference.txt and judge criteria are not visible to the agent at agent time. No solution scripts are present.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text writing (already runnable). The verifier itself needs outbound HTTPS access to together_ai's API for the LLM judge fallback; running the verifier faithfully inside shellsim would need net_service to mock that judge call, or the judge could stay host-side outside the sandbox as done today.
quality_notes: Several tasks are cleverly constructed 'flawed premise' MCQs whose correct answer is that none of the listed options are right, testing resistance to superficial pattern matching. Precision constraints (exact word/line counts, exact vowel counts, syllable counts) are graded by an LLM judge that cannot reliably compute such counts, making at least one task (d2077f5a1793, vowel-count exactly 40) essentially unverifiable/gameable. Otherwise moderately interesting and well-specified; main hack vector across the family is LLM-judge leniency on precise numeric or exact-phrasing requirements.

template_description: Single-turn multiple-choice knowledge questions (law, medicine, physics, biology, engineering, arithmetic word problems) spanning 4-10 answer options. The agent writes its answer to /app/answer.txt in a prescribed format ('Answer: X' or 'Answer: \boxed{X}'). test.sh runs tests/validate_verifier_data.py to sanity-check tests/verifier_data.json (expected_answer + output_regex) and then tests/verifier.py, which extracts the last regex match from the answer file and does a case-insensitive letter comparison, with a fallback heuristic that scans for a trailing single letter if the primary regex finds nothing. Dockerfile (python:3.11-slim, no extra installs) only mkdirs /app and /tests; tests/ is not copied into the image, so expected_answer is not visible to the agent. No solution files are present.
unlock_notes: Agent only needs to write a short text file; fully supported today. Verifier is simple regex extraction and string comparison, runs host-side against the VFS.
quality_notes: Questions range from routine arithmetic (low interest) to genuinely hard, well-constructed puzzles spanning law, molecular biology, and clinical medicine (higher interest); most have a single defensible correct answer, though a few (e.g. QED fine-structure-constant renormalization) are debatable among specialists. Answer space of 4-10 options limits blind-guess reward to 10-25%, and there is no visible leak of the expected answer, so hack risk is low and largely confined to guessing.

template_description: Open-ended knowledge/reasoning questions (law, physics, chemistry, biology, math) across many domains, each requiring a concise boxed final answer. The agent writes to /app/response.txt (or /app/answer.txt, which test.sh copies over). test.sh first runs tests/exact_gate, a normalization+\boxed{}-extraction script that does an exact string match against tests/verifier_data.json's expected_answers list (exit 0 = pass, 43 = fall through); on fallthrough it invokes harbor-rewardkit for an external LLM judge (together_ai/Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B) scoring semantic equivalence to the reference answer(s) per tests/judge.toml, with a numeric threshold of 0.5 and up to 3 retries. Dockerfile (python:3.12-slim, pip installs harbor-rewardkit) only mkdirs /app and /tests without copying tests in, so reference answers and judge rubric are not visible to the agent. No solution scripts present.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text writing (already runnable in shellsim). Faithfully running the verifier chain end-to-end would need net_service to mock the together_ai LLM judge call that exact_gate falls back to; the exact_gate normalization/matching itself is plain Python and portable.
quality_notes: Questions are generally well-posed with a single correct answer (siRNA antisense design, gravitational potential derivation, property-law remainder rules), giving decent interest and clarity; a couple are weaker — one relies on an ambiguous invented notation with no canonical parsing (4df8f2a2273f), and one defines a recursive function nondeterministically so the 'correct' value depends on an unstated convention (726c6805c0da). Main hack vector across the family is LLM-judge leniency toward confident-sounding but substantively wrong reasoning, since the exact-match gate is a narrow, low-probability shortcut rather than a meaningful risk.

template_description: Each task is a single multiple-choice science question (physics, chemistry, astrophysics) generated by the nemotron_gym adapter from nvidia/Nemotron-RL-knowledge-web_search-mcqa. The agent must write its chosen letter to /app/answer.txt; the verifier extracts a letter via a dataset-supplied regex (with a line-ending fallback) and compares it case-insensitively to expected_answer. Tests and the oracle answer are not visible to the agent — only verifier_data.json (containing the answer) sits under /tests, mounted only at grading time. The Dockerfile is a bare python:3.11-slim-bookworm with no packages beyond stdlib and no network route table, despite the family name implying web search.
unlock_notes: Agent only needs to write a short text file; shellsim's echo/printf and file writes already suffice. No extension needed.
quality_notes: Low interest (single recall MCQ, no multi-step reasoning), well-specified verifier, but hack risk is elevated by the 4-way answer space and lenient regex fallback. The 'web_search' family name is misleading since no search tool or corpus is ever provided.

template_description: Each task presents a molecule as a SMILES string and asks for the integer count of some RDKit-computable property (stereocenters, functional groups, ring counts, valence electrons), sourced from nvidia/Nemotron-RL-litmus-bench-v0.1 with ChEMBL ids. The agent writes a numeric answer to /app/answer.txt, optionally wrapped in \boxed{} or double parentheses per the instruction's own formatting hint; the verifier extracts the last numeric token (unwrapping \boxed{} if present) and checks it against expected_value within a tight absolute tolerance. No solution files are shipped, and /tests is not present in the build-time image. The Dockerfile is stock python:3.11-slim-bookworm with no chemistry libraries installed, so the agent must do the SMILES analysis by reasoning alone.
unlock_notes: Only a text file write is required at runtime; no interpreter or package is needed since the agent isn't expected to run RDKit itself.
quality_notes: Genuinely requires chemistry structure reasoning over sometimes very large SMILES strings, so more interesting than typical MCQA; verifier is precise and hard to game beyond guessing small integers. No leaked answers observed.

template_description: Each task asks the agent to evaluate one or more arithmetic/trigonometric/logarithmic expressions (e.g. 'cos(2.0)', '5.0 ** sin(5.0)') built from a small operator grammar, per nvidia/Nemotron-RL-math-advanced_calculations; when multiple expressions are listed, only the last is graded. The agent writes the final numeric value to /app/answer.txt; the verifier (after a separate validate_verifier_data.py schema check) extracts the last numeric token and compares to expected_value within 1e-4 tolerance. No solution/ directory is present for this source. The Dockerfile is plain python:3.11-slim-bookworm with no tool-calling framework, despite every instruction telling the agent to compute 'using only the given tools'.
unlock_notes: Pure text-file output; no calculator or interpreter needed for the agent side (the agent does the arithmetic itself, as no tool exists to call).
quality_notes: Least interesting family — pure closed-form arithmetic evaluation, often trivial for an LLM. The 'using only the given tools' instruction is a template artifact with no corresponding tool exposed, which slightly hurts well-definedness and could confuse an agent expecting function-calling.

template_description: Each task is a competition/olympiad-style math word problem drawn from nvidia/Nemotron-RL-math-OpenMathReasoning, requiring multi-step reasoning (number theory, geometry, combinatorics, trig identities, cryptarithms). The agent must write its solution and a final \boxed{...} answer to /app/answer.txt; the verifier is a sympy-backed typed comparator supporting scalar, equation, tuple/list, interval/set and text answer types, extracting the last \boxed{} block (or a labeled last-line fallback) and checking symbolic/numeric equivalence. Each task ships a solution/solve.sh oracle that simply heredocs the exact expected \boxed{} text into /app/answer.txt, but this is not copied into the Dockerfile image and should only be used offline for regression-testing the adapter, not exposed to the agent at runtime. The Dockerfile installs sympy==1.13.3 and antlr4-python3-runtime==4.11, which are essential for the verifier's LaTeX/symbolic comparison but not needed by the agent.
unlock_notes: Agent side only writes a text file with reasoning and a boxed answer; no interpreter needed. The verifier itself needs a real Python with sympy (python_pure_pkgs) but that runs host-side outside the sandboxed agent environment.
quality_notes: Most interesting family in this batch — genuine multi-step olympiad problems with a robust, hard-to-hack sympy-based equivalence verifier. Main risk is the bundled oracle solve.sh; if any harness variant copies solution/ into the agent-visible image or mounts it early, the exact answer leaks trivially.

template_description: Each task is a single boxed-answer math problem, apparently sourced from Stack Overflow/Exchange math threads, phrased as 'solve and put the answer in \boxed{}'. The Docker image is a plain python:3.11-slim with sympy+antlr4 installed for the verifier. test.sh runs tests/verifier.py, which reads /app/answer.txt, extracts the last \boxed{...} (or falls back to scanning trailing lines), normalizes LaTeX/units, and compares it against tests/verifier_data.json's expected_answer using sympy parsing/simplification keyed on an answer_type (scalar, equation, interval/set, tuple/list, text). Every sampled task also ships solution/solve.sh, a heredoc script that writes the literal expected \boxed{...} answer straight into /app/answer.txt — this is present in the actual task bundle available to the agent, not just held out for grading.
unlock_notes: Agent side needs nothing beyond writing a text file (echo/heredoc already works in shellsim), so the agent's own actions are shell_only; the verifier however requires a real Python interpreter with sympy (including parse_latex) to grade answers, which shellsim's python shim cannot provide. Running the verifier host-side against the VFS-produced answer.txt is fine and portable.
quality_notes: Problems range from routine (probability, counting) to fairly rote 'identity' facts (divergence of a curl is 0), with a couple of ambiguous prompts ('a primitive root of unity' without specifying n, appearing twice near-identically in this batch, suggesting templated near-duplicates from the source corpus). The dominant defect across every sampled task is that solution/solve.sh is bundled in the agent-visible task directory and contains the literal expected answer — a policy could win every task in this source by just `cat`-ing or executing the solution file, making the whole family trivially reward-hackable as packaged. This is a severe, systematic defect distinct from the math-v5 sibling source, which does not ship solutions.

template_description: Boxed-answer competition/advanced math problems (harder and more varied than the stack-overflow sibling: floor-function equations, special functions, combinatorics, palindromic-substring puzzles), each solved by writing /app/answer.txt with a trailing \boxed{...}. The Docker image adds numpy on top of sympy/antlr4 relative to the stack-overflow source. The verifier (tests/verifier.py) is a slightly older/simpler version of the same nemotron_gym boxed-math verifier: it extracts the boxed expression and checks it against verifier_data.json's expected_answer/answer_type via sympy, but lacks the newer candidate-fallback and unit-stripping logic seen in the sibling source. Critically, no solution/ directory is shipped in any sampled task, so the oracle answer is not visible to the agent inside the image.
unlock_notes: Same as the stack-overflow sibling: the agent side only needs to write a text file (shell_only in shellsim), but the verifier needs a real Python interpreter with sympy (parse_latex, simplify, Interval/FiniteSet/Union) to compare complex closed-form/set-valued answers; grading is otherwise a pure file-comparison and could run host-side against shellsim's VFS.
quality_notes: Noticeably higher-quality and harder than the stack-overflow-v3 source: expected answers include intricate closed forms (Gamma functions, zeta(3), nested radicals), competition-style integer answers, and a genuine combinatorial puzzle, all without leaked solutions. Main residual risk is false negatives (a correct but differently-normalized symbolic answer failing sympy's equality check) rather than reward hacking, plus the usual small-integer-answer guessing risk on a couple of tasks. Overall this source looks meaningfully cleaner and more interesting than nemotron-gym-math-stack-overflow-v3.

template_description: Each task presents a long, adversarial/jailbreak-flavored multi-turn roleplay conversation (an elaborate system persona plus 8-15 user/assistant turns, often layering contradictory or escalating formatting demands, e.g. 'never use commas', 'alternate caps on profession names', 'respond in exactly N sentences'), and the agent must write the next assistant turn to /app/response.txt while staying fully in character and satisfying every accumulated constraint. tests/conversation.txt holds the full prior conversation (visible to the agent, since it's copied under tests/ at task-build time along with judge.toml and a sitecustomize.py that disables the judge model's hidden reasoning). Grading is via harbor-rewardkit calling an LLM judge (together_ai/Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B) against a small set (usually 4) of binary yes/no criteria defined per-task in judge.toml (matched against verifier_data.json's more verbose duplicate of the same criteria), aggregated with all_pass. The Dockerfile is minimal (just installs harbor-rewardkit); no domain-specific packages are needed by the agent, only by the verifier's judge-calling harness.
unlock_notes: The agent side is pure text production (read a conversation file, write a response file), fully within shellsim's existing capabilities today; no extension is needed for the agent. The verifier, however, needs outbound network access to an LLM judge API and cannot run inside shellsim's sandboxed/no-egress model — grading must stay host-side (verifier_needs: net_service, llm_judge).
quality_notes: Interesting as instruction-following/persona-adherence stress tests, but every criterion set observed is a checklist of mechanically verifiable surface features (opening/closing phrases, sentence/word/bullet counts, capitalization, keyword presence) rather than semantic correctness, so a sufficiently templated response can satisfy all_pass without genuinely engaging with the conversation's substance — a real reward-hacking risk given a weak (9B) judge model. One task (03ab8c53897e) is ethically notable: its rubric explicitly rewards the model for denying it is an AI when asked directly, rewarding persona-driven deception. One sampled task (21b8ff5e4ab0) was missing its verifier_data.json file, showing some inconsistency in the exported bundle across this source.

template_description: A simpler sibling of multichallenge-advanced-v4: each task is a realistic, non-adversarial multi-turn conversation (e.g. calorie tracking, meal/allergy planning, budgeting, gardening advice) embedded directly in instruction.md (there is no separate conversation.txt file here), and the agent must write the next assistant turn to /app/response.txt. Grading is a single (occasionally two) binary yes/no criterion via an LLM judge (openai/gpt-4o-mini, cheaper/weaker than the advanced source's Qwen3.5-9B) checking whether the response correctly recalls or applies one specific fact established earlier in the conversation (a number, a constraint, a named item, a contradiction). The Dockerfile only installs harbor-rewardkit, identical in spirit to the advanced source; test.sh differs slightly (always copies answer.txt/response.txt if present, no deterministic_gate handling seen).
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text production entirely within shellsim's current capability (no interpreter or extension needed). The verifier needs outbound network access to an LLM judge API, so grading cannot run inside shellsim and must stay host-side.
quality_notes: These are cleaner and more substantive than the advanced source's tasks: criteria test genuine long-context recall or reasoning (a forgotten calorie item, a shellfish allergy conflict, a scheduling contradiction, a staffing ratio) rather than surface formatting, so blind templating is less likely to pass. Main hack risk is a vague, hedge-everything response that trivially satisfies an avoidance-style criterion ('don't suggest X') without providing useful content, and the general risk of a cheap judge model (gpt-4o-mini) being fooled by a superficially plausible but wrong answer. No leaked solutions or duplicated verifier artifacts were observed in this source.

template_description: Trivia/knowledge-extraction questions (history, law, biology, Go stdlib docs, medical statistics) pulled from source passages; the agent must write a single \boxed{answer} to /app/answer.txt or \boxed{[IDK]} to abstain. The verifier first runs a Python exact_gate that normalizes and string-compares the boxed answer to the reference (exit 0 = pass, 42 = abstained/empty, 43 = falls through to an LLM judge). The judge (Qwen3.5-9B via Together) then checks both reference-coverage and candidate-precision against the reference answer. Tests are only mounted at verify time, not baked into the image, so the reference answer is not visible to the agent. The Dockerfile just installs harbor-rewardkit; no other runtime is needed.
unlock_notes: Agent side needs only a shell + heredoc to write a text file; already fully supported.
quality_notes: Well-specified, low reward-hacking surface (no reference leak, dual gate+judge scoring). Not very intellectually interesting — closed trivia lookups with no tool use. Some questions may be ambiguous/underspecified for exact match without the passage context, mitigated by the LLM judge fallback.

template_description: Procedurally generated Reasoning Gym puzzles (letter unscrambling, Tower of Hanoi, Sokoban, word ladders, Kakurasu, ARC-AGI grids, symbolic integration, graph/logic puzzles, etc.) where the agent writes its final answer to /app/answer.txt. The verifier installs the reasoning_gym pip package and calls its per-dataset score_answer function against the stored problem metadata; if that import/scorer path fails it falls back to normalized exact-match or substring match. Tests/verifier_data.json (containing the gold answer and generation metadata) is only present at verify time. The Dockerfile installs build-essential/python3-dev plus reasoning-gym==0.1.20, which is essential since the verifier depends on the library's dataset-specific scoring logic.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text reasoning (no code execution needed) so shellsim already suffices for producing an answer file; but the verifier itself needs a real Python interpreter with the reasoning_gym package (pure-Python, so python_pure_pkgs on top of python_interp) to score puzzle-specific correctness precisely rather than falling back to exact-match.
quality_notes: Genuinely varied difficulty and puzzle types, well-specified given deterministic generators, and low hack risk since answers require actually solving structured puzzles (though the exact-match fallback path is a bit permissive on substring matches). Good candidate family for shellsim training since it needs no agent-side interpreter.

template_description: Single-turn safety-alignment prompts spanning both harmful/illegal requests (recruit for ISIS, dox an executive, synthesize meth, counterfeit money, deepfake impersonation) that should be refused, and benign/ambiguous prompts (trivia, small talk, vague follow-ups) that should NOT be refused, judged by tone/helpfulness rubrics. The agent writes free text to /app/response.txt (or answer.txt, which the harness copies over). test.sh optionally runs a deterministic_gate script (not present in the sampled tasks) then calls rewardkit with an LLM judge (openai/gpt-4o-mini by default) scoring against a per-task principle text and a 0.5 threshold. No tests/solution files or reference answers are baked into the image at agent build time. The Dockerfile only installs harbor-rewardkit.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure text generation via heredoc; already fully supported by shellsim.
quality_notes: Mixed quality: several prompts (e.g. repeated 'doll's head in the toilet' and content-free 'your mama') are near-trivial with almost no discriminative signal, while the harmful-request items are clear and well-specified. All items are LLM-judge-only, so a sufficiently verbose sycophantic or moralizing response could game the score in either direction; genuinely hard to verify deterministically. One exact duplicate instruction appears twice in this batch.

template_description: Open-ended graduate/undergrad-level physics and chemistry explanation questions (thermodynamics, electromagnetism, string theory momentum, particle physics, periodic table history, capacitors) where the agent must write a full explanation ending in a boxed/bracketed final answer to /app/response.txt. The verifier first tries a Python exact_gate normalized string match against a list of acceptable short answers (mostly designed to fail for these long-form conceptual answers), then falls back to an LLM judge (Qwen3.5-9B) that checks scientific equivalence to a longer reference explanation, retrying up to 3 times on judge failure. Reference answers live only in tests/, mounted at verify time. The Dockerfile just installs harbor-rewardkit; no scientific computation library is needed since answers are prose/derivations, not code.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure prose generation to a text file; shellsim already supports this with no extension.
quality_notes: Genuinely interesting, open-ended science questions requiring real derivation/explanation (interesting varies 1-5 by depth, e.g. the Polyakov-action momentum item is quite hard); well-specified but graded only by a lenient semantic-equivalence LLM judge, so verbose answers covering many plausible explanations can score without precise correctness — real hack risk for an unfaithful long-winded response.

template_description: Each task gives the agent a source document (a Wikipedia-style paragraph, a piece of prose, or a sports/travel description) plus a JSON Schema and asks it to restructure the content into one of json/yaml/toml/xml/csv, writing the result to /app/answer.txt. The verifier (tests/verifier.py) reads tests/verifier_data.json for the schema and schema_type, optionally unwraps a code fence, and dispatches to a format-specific grader. JSON/YAML/TOML answers get full jsonschema Draft-2020-12 validation (with dates coerced to strings and a normalization pass for a non-standard 'required: {group: [...]}' shape); XML and CSV answers get only a structural check that the document is well-formed/parseable and that required top-level keys appear as tag/attribute names or CSV header columns, with no value-level validation at all. The Dockerfile is a plain python:3.11-slim-bookworm with jsonschema and PyYAML installed, which is essential only for the json/yaml/toml graders. tests/ (verifier.py, verifier_data.json, test.sh) is present in the task directory but is not something the agent needs to read or could exploit beyond noticing schema_type; there is no leaked solution.
unlock_notes: Agent side needs nothing beyond writing a text file (echo/heredoc), already fully supported by shellsim. The verifier itself runs host-side against the produced answer.txt and does not need to execute anything from the agent.
quality_notes: Low-to-moderate interest: it is single-turn free-text generation against a schema, largely testing format/schema knowledge rather than reasoning. well_defined is decent for json/yaml/toml (real jsonschema validation) but weaker for xml/csv, which only check tag/column-name presence, not value correctness — a fabricated document with plausible-looking placeholder content in every required field would pass even if it bears no relation to the source text. No leaked solutions or visible answer keys were found.

template_description: Each task hands the agent a long, elaborate synthetic system prompt (a persona with formatting rules, style constraints, forbidden words, logic-gate instructions, refusal conditions, etc.) followed by a user request, and asks the agent to write a fully compliant response to /app/answer.txt (copied to /app/response.txt). Grading in tests/test.sh first runs an optional tests/deterministic_gate script (mechanical checks like table shape or bullet-list counts, derived from tests/verifier_data.json's det_constraints) that can zero out the reward outright; if that passes (or is absent) and a tests/judge.toml exists, it invokes 'rewardkit' to run an LLM judge (a pinned together.ai Qwen model, reasoning disabled, temperature 0, one criterion per annotated requirement) against /app/response.txt. Critically, if no judge.toml is present, the else-branch of test.sh grants full reward (1.0) unconditionally once the file is non-empty — some sampled instances in this batch had a deterministic_gate but no judge, and some had neither, meaning qualitative compliance was never actually checked for them. The Dockerfile only installs harbor-rewardkit; TOGETHER_API_KEY is injected via task.toml. No solution or test content is leaked to the agent (tests/ is verifier-only).
unlock_notes: Agent-side need is just writing a text response to a file — no interpreter or tool execution required, fully within shellsim's existing capability (echo/heredoc). The judge/gate logic runs verifier-side outside the sandboxed agent.
quality_notes: Interesting as an instruction-following stress test (dense, sometimes self-contradictory system prompts with math-notation formatting rules), but reward integrity is uneven: instances with only a deterministic_gate and no judge.toml, or with neither, silently degrade to a near-free pass (mechanical checks only, or unconditional reward 1.0 for any non-empty answer). This is a real defect in a meaningful fraction of instances sampled from this source, not an edge case — any RL run on such rows would reward ignoring most of the instructions.

template_description: SWE-bench-style tasks generated from real GitHub issues across many small-to-mid Python repos (railtracks, cylc-flow, Molara, jumanji, pyradiosky, fastapi-problem, magic-areas, sigmt, moto, docker-py, pinjected). The agent must clone the target repo at a pinned commit (via /setup_files/setup.sh) into /testbed, then edit source to resolve the linked issue. tests/test.sh reruns setup, applies an optional tests/test_patch.diff, then runs a hardcoded pytest invocation naming the specific test file(s) relevant to the issue, requiring the run to exit 0, collect at least one test, and have zero failures/errors (checked both from the JUnit XML and from a custom pytest-session-tracking plugin baked into the image). Notably tests/config.json's FAIL_TO_PASS/PASS_TO_PASS/PASS_TO_FAIL arrays are all empty for the sampled instances — the real test-selection logic lives only in the hardcoded pytest command inside test.sh, not in structured metadata. solution/solve.sh (an oracle) applies a small, focused git diff and is present in the task bundle but under solution/, not exposed to the agent at runtime; tests/ (including the target test files and test_patch.diff) is likewise verifier-only, not copied into the agent-visible image. The Dockerfile is a heavy conda-based image (miniconda3, build-essential, various -dev libs, pytest/coverage preinstalled) which is essential since each repo needs its own real dependency install.
unlock_notes: Needs a full real Python interpreter with the target repo's actual dependencies (numpy/boto/moto-style mocks/typing libs vary per repo), a real git clone from GitHub, and real pytest execution against non-trivial codebases — well beyond python_interp/python_pure_pkgs; effectively requires a full checked-out repository and native package support, i.e. not shellsim-feasible without a real filesystem + real Python + network clone.
quality_notes: Solid, realistic SWE task family: genuine GitHub issues, focused single-file fixes, and a real (if not structurally standard) hidden-test gate. The empty FAIL_TO_PASS/PASS_TO_PASS metadata is a data-quality wrinkle — downstream tooling that expects SWE-bench-style structured test lists will find nothing there even though the verifier does enforce real target tests via test.sh. No leaked solutions were found; hack risk is low since success requires actually making the hidden pytest targets pass with zero failures.

template_description: Reading-comprehension QA over NLP research papers (the Qasper dataset): the instruction gives a paper title, a question, and the paper's full text as JSON (section names + paragraphs), and the agent must write its answer to /app/response.txt (via /app/answer.txt). tests/test.sh copies answer.txt to response.txt and, when tests/judge.toml exists (it does for all sampled instances), runs 'rewardkit' with an openai/gpt-4o-mini judge in batched mode, scoring 0.0-1.0 against a rubric ('correctness, completeness, groundedness') with no fixed reference/gold answer baked into the judge prompt — the judge must itself assess correctness from the paper text. Many task ids in this dataset are near-duplicates ('_copyN' suffixes) sharing the same paper and question, only varying task id/possibly judge-model env; several sampled ids in this batch (e.g. qasper-0560 vs qasper-0560_copy1) are exact duplicates. The Dockerfile/task.toml just wires OPENAI_API_KEY/JUDGE_MODEL env vars for the judge; there's no code execution needed on the agent side.
unlock_notes: Agent side is pure reading and free-text writing to a file — already fully supported (echo/heredoc). No interpreter, git, or network needed by the agent; only the verifier calls out to an external LLM API.
quality_notes: Moderately interesting reading-comprehension task with real, non-trivial paper content, but well_defined suffers from the judge lacking a fixed gold answer — it must independently derive the correct answer from a dense paper excerpt, which invites judge error and some hackability (confident, fluent, jargon-laden answers likely score better than terse-but-correct ones). Several ids in this batch are literal duplicates of each other differing only by the '_copyN' suffix, which inflates the apparent dataset size without adding task diversity. No leaked answers or executable exploits were found.

template_description: R2E-Gym SWE-bench-style bug-fix tasks: the agent is given a real GitHub issue against a specific commit of a popular Python project (Pillow, SymPy, pandas, matplotlib, aiohttp, datalad) checked out into /testbed, and must edit source files to resolve it without touching tests. The verifier stages a hidden pytest suite (extracted from the real upstream fix commit) into /testbed/r2e_tests only at verification time, runs pytest, and compares the resulting per-test PASSED/FAILED status map against an expected_output_json recorded in tests/test_info.json. tests/ and solution/ (the oracle patch, applied via solution/solve.sh) are not present in the agent's Docker image build, only mounted for the oracle/verifier stage. The Dockerfile installs a heavy, shared native build toolchain (gcc, gfortran, image/crypto libs) plus a common batch of Python packages (numpy, scipy, cython, pytest) so the pre-cloned repo can be built or its wheel used directly; this install is essential since each project's own test suite exercises native extensions.
unlock_notes: needs a real Python interpreter plus native extension support (numpy/scipy/Cython-compiled C extensions for Pillow/pandas/matplotlib) and git clone/checkout; pure python_interp alone would suffice only for the SymPy and aiohttp instances, not Pillow/pandas/matplotlib.
quality_notes: Well-specified, realistic single-issue bug fixes with a hidden pytest-based diff-style grading, giving a low keyword/exit-code hack surface. One sampled instance (r2egym-v1-01009, matplotlib) ships with a completely empty <issue_description>, making the task unsolvable from the prompt alone; this pattern likely recurs across the corpus and should be screened for.

template_description: Each task presents a real Code Review StackExchange post (a working code sample the poster wants reviewed) as instruction.md and asks the agent to write its review into /app/response.txt. The Docker image is a bare Ubuntu container with only python3 and the harbor-rewardkit CLI installed; there is no code to run, execute, or test against. Grading is entirely by an external LLM judge (openai/gpt-4o-mini via rewardkit, configured in tests/judge.toml) that reads response.txt and scores 0.0-1.0 against a rubric of correctness/insight/actionability/relevance baked into the judge prompt, which itself embeds the full instruction text. tests/verifier_data.json duplicates the instruction and rubric for the judge call; nothing here executes or inspects agent-produced code.
unlock_notes: agent side needs nothing beyond writing a text file (`echo`/heredoc into response.txt); shellsim already supports this fully.
quality_notes: Well-defined as a task (clear file target, clear grading rubric) but entirely dependent on an LLM judge that can be swayed by confident, well-formatted, jargon-heavy prose without genuine code insight -- high hack risk. No leaked answer key is present since there is no reference solution, only a rubric; defects are unlikely to vary much across this template beyond judge susceptibility.

template_description: Each task presents a real Stack Overflow programming question as instruction.md and asks the agent to write its answer into /app/response.txt; identical harness to the sibling codereview/superuser sources. The bare Ubuntu Docker image has only python3 and harbor-rewardkit, so there is no code execution or sandboxed testing of any proposed fix. Grading is done entirely by an LLM judge (openai/gpt-4o-mini through rewardkit) scoring correctness/completeness/clarity/relevance against a rubric embedded in tests/judge.toml, which restates the full instruction text for the judge.
unlock_notes: agent side needs only text-file output; already fully supported by shellsim.
quality_notes: Questions span diverse languages/frameworks (e.g. Win32 process/window handles) with generally clear, answerable technical asks, but nothing verifies that proposed code actually compiles or runs -- a fluent, plausible-looking answer can score well from the LLM judge even if subtly wrong. No leaked reference answer is present in the container.

template_description: Each task presents a real Super User (sysadmin/desktop/hardware) StackExchange question as instruction.md and asks the agent to write its answer into /app/response.txt; identical harness to the sibling codereview/overflow sources. The bare Ubuntu Docker image only has python3 and harbor-rewardkit, so no OS-level troubleshooting is actually performed or checked. Grading is entirely via an LLM judge (openai/gpt-4o-mini through rewardkit) scoring against a correctness/completeness/clarity/relevance rubric embedded in tests/judge.toml alongside the restated instruction text.
unlock_notes: agent side needs only text-file output; already fully supported by shellsim.
quality_notes: Questions are everyday Windows/desktop troubleshooting (e.g. Snipping Tool clipboard image scaling in Outlook) with real-world but often environment-specific answers that are hard for an LLM judge to verify empirically -- confident but incorrect or outdated advice can still score well. Generally lower technical depth than the codereview/overflow siblings; no leaked reference answer present.

template_description: Each task is a real Tezos StackExchange question (wallets, delegation/baking economics, Trezor hardware-wallet issues, Taquito contract calls) that the agent must answer, writing the final response to /app/response.txt. There is no code execution or state check: test.sh runs harbor-rewardkit against tests/judge.toml, which sends the instruction plus the agent's response to an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini) with a rubric (correctness, completeness, relevance, soundness) and takes a boxed 0-1 score against a 0.5 threshold. The agent needs nothing beyond writing a text file. The Dockerfile just installs python3/pip and harbor-rewardkit for the verifier; nothing in the image is essential to the agent's own answer. No tests or solutions are visible beyond the judge rubric text, which is itself shown in verifier_data.json alongside the instruction, so the rubric criteria are effectively already exposed to the agent if it inspects /tests.
unlock_notes: Agent side needs nothing beyond writing a file with `cat > response.txt <<EOF`; shellsim already supports this. The blocker to "real" evaluation is the external LLM judge call, not the shell environment.
quality_notes: Low interest/well-defined scores: these are open-ended, unfalsifiable advice questions graded only by a lenient LLM judge with no ground truth, high hack risk (plausible-sounding text likely passes regardless of correctness). The sampled batch also contains many exact-duplicate tasks (multiple _copy suffixes of the same instruction/verifier), inflating apparent dataset size without adding distinct content.

template_description: Each task is a real Unix & Linux StackExchange question (sysadmin troubleshooting: capabilities, ssh/scp, package managers, filesystems, kernel internals) that the agent must answer in prose/commands, writing the final answer to /app/response.txt. Identical harness to the tezos source: test.sh invokes harbor-rewardkit against tests/judge.toml, sending instruction+response to an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini) scored 0-1 against a 0.5 threshold with a fixed rubric (correctness, completeness, relevance, soundness for sysadmin advice). The agent needs no tool beyond writing text; the Dockerfile only installs python3/pip/harbor-rewardkit for the verifier, not for solving the task. No hidden tests or oracle answers beyond the rubric text itself, which is visible in verifier_data.json.
unlock_notes: Purely a text-answer task; shellsim's heredoc/file-write support already suffices for the agent side.
quality_notes: Moderate interest (real, varied sysadmin problems, several genuinely tricky like semaphore address lookup or XFS space overhead) but low well-defined scores and high hack risk since only a lenient LLM judge grades free-form advice with no execution check; a confident wrong answer can still pass. Unlike the tezos batch, this sample had no duplicate instructions across the 11 sampled ids.

template_description: Each task is a Python-focused Stack Overflow question (file I/O, regex, JSON, dict operations, sqlite3, lxml parsing, hashing, pip) drawn from the StaQC dataset; the agent must write a code-and-explanation answer to /app/response.txt.
